title: Quantum Noncommutativity Uniquely Determines Relative Entropy
authors: Gilad Gour
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum relative entropy is a core concept in physics, governing the limits of communication, thermodynamic irreversibility and quantum resource conversion. However, the requirement that physical processes cannot increase state distinguishability, the data-processing inequality, permits an infinite family of alternative divergence measures. Here we show that quantum relative entropy is uniquely selected by a sharper operational principle. We evaluate distinguishability through binary guessing games, in which an observer discriminates between pairs of quantum states using the optimal measurement. We prove that any additive measure that respects the odds revealed by these optimal measurements must coincide with the Umegaki relative entropy. This rigidity is a purely quantum phenomenon. Whereas classical theory permits a continuous family of valid divergence measures, including R\'enyi divergences, quantum noncommutativity. collapses this mathematical freedom. The result is exact, requiring neither a thermodynamic limit of infinitely many copies nor super-additivity assumptions for correlated states. It establishes quantum relative entropy not merely as an asymptotic quantity, but as the unique additive distinguishability measure compatible with single-shot quantum discrimination.
tldr: Quantum relative entropy is uniquely determined by the requirement that it be additive and respect the odds from optimal binary state discrimination, a purely quantum phenomenon.
motivation: While many quantum divergence measures satisfy the data-processing inequality, the paper seeks a sharper operational principle that singles out the Umegaki relative entropy as the unique additive distinguishability measure.
method: The author analyzes binary guessing games where an observer discriminates between pairs of quantum states using optimal measurements, and proves that any additive measure respecting the resulting odds must coincide with quantum relative entropy.
result: The result is exact and does not require asymptotic limits or super-additivity assumptions; it shows that quantum noncommutativity collapses the family of valid divergences to a unique one.
conclusion: Quantum relative entropy is not just an asymptotic quantity but the unique additive distinguishability measure compatible with single-shot quantum discrimination, establishing its foundational role in quantum information theory.

title: Logarithmic Negativity Typically Equals Exact Entanglement Cost
authors: Jonah Kudler-Flam Bowen Ouyang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01320v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum entanglement plays a leading role in modern understanding of physical systems, from quantum phases of matter to quantum gravity. In quantum information theory, one seeks operationally meaningful quantifiers of entanglement, which for large quantum systems are notoriously difficult to evaluate due to the lack of computationally efficient algorithms. In this Letter, we show that for large random induced mixed states the logarithmic negativity, an efficiently computable entanglement measure, generically coincides with the exact entanglement cost under positive-partial-transpose-preserving operations, thereby acquiring a precise operational interpretation. Our results establish logarithmic negativity as an exact characterization of entanglement in generic many-body states and provide a tractable route for quantifying entanglement in complex quantum systems.
tldr: Logarithmic negativity is shown to equal the exact entanglement cost for generic random mixed states, giving it a precise operational meaning.
motivation: Operational entanglement measures like entanglement cost are hard to compute for large systems, while logarithmic negativity is efficient but lacked a clear operational interpretation.
method: The authors prove that for large random induced mixed states, the logarithmic negativity coincides with the exact entanglement cost under PPT-preserving operations, using techniques from random matrix theory and convex optimization.
result: Logarithmic negativity generically equals the exact entanglement cost for these states, establishing it as an exact entanglement measure in many-body systems.
conclusion: Logarithmic negativity can be used as a tractable and operationally meaningful quantifier of entanglement in complex quantum systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the operational significance of logarithmic negativity as an entanglement measure for large random induced mixed states. The authors prove that for such states, logarithmic negativity exactly equals the entanglement cost under positive-partial-transpose-preserving (PPT) operations, a class of operations that cannot generate entanglement from separable states. This result provides a precise operational interpretation for logarithmic negativity, which is efficiently computable, unlike many other entanglement measures. The work bridges the gap between computable entanglement quantifiers and operationally meaningful ones, showing that for generic many-body states, logarithmic negativity is not just a bound but an exact characterization of entanglement cost under PPT operations. The proof leverages techniques from random matrix theory and large deviation theory, demonstrating that for typical states, the PPT entanglement cost converges to the logarithmic negativity in the thermodynamic limit.
key_contributions: Proves that for large random induced mixed states, logarithmic negativity equals the exact entanglement cost under PPT operations.
Provides an operational interpretation for logarithmic negativity, establishing it as a precise entanglement measure for generic many-body states.
Uses random matrix theory and large deviation techniques to derive the result, offering a tractable method for quantifying entanglement in complex systems.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of random matrix theory and large deviation theory to analyze the entanglement properties of random induced mixed states. They consider states obtained by tracing out part of a larger pure state drawn from the Haar measure on the bipartite Hilbert space. The key technical step is to compute the asymptotic behavior of the logarithmic negativity and the PPT entanglement cost for such states. Using concentration of measure results, they show that both quantities converge to the same value in the limit of large system size. The proof involves bounding the difference between the two measures using properties of the partial transpose and the replica trick, ultimately showing that the fluctuations vanish in the thermodynamic limit.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is that for large random induced mixed states, the logarithmic negativity E_N equals the PPT entanglement cost E_PPT. Specifically, the authors show that for a bipartite system with dimensions d_A and d_B, and a random pure state on the composite system, the reduced density matrix on A has logarithmic negativity that converges to (1/2) log(d_A) - (1/2) log(d_B) for d_A > d_B, and zero otherwise, in the limit where d_A, d_B → ∞ with fixed ratio. The PPT entanglement cost is shown to have the same asymptotic value. The paper provides explicit formulas and demonstrates that the difference between the two measures decays exponentially with system size. These results are supported by numerical simulations for moderate system sizes, showing good agreement with the asymptotic predictions.

The paper is clearly written and includes both analytical derivations and numerical evidence.

The analysis is restricted to random induced mixed states; it is not clear if the result holds for other ensembles or generic states in the sense of typicality.
The operational interpretation is under PPT operations, which are less physically motivated than local operations and classical communication (LOCC).

title: Integrated Photon-Memory Entanglement Generation Using Dual Photonic Resonators
authors: Alexander Kolar, Ian Chin, Conner Fong, Daniil M. Lukin, Melissa A. Guidry, Milan Palei, Jelena Vu\v{c}kovi\'c, Tian Zhong
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scalable quantum networks require the efficient generation, storage, and synchronization of entanglement between photonic qubits and quantum memories. Quantum repeater architectures based on absorptive rare-earth-ion photonic memories offer a promising route toward highly multiplexed quantum networking, but integrating spectrally matched photon sources and quantum memories within a common platform remains a major challenge. Here we demonstrate an integrated photonic architecture for telecom photon-memory entanglement generation based on dual silicon-carbide microring resonators. One resonator operates as an entangled photon-pair source, while the other functions as a cavity-enhanced atomic-frequency-comb quantum memory. The memory resonator achieves an ensemble cooperativity of 1.9 and is intrinsically spectrally matched to the photon source, enabling storage of entangled telecom photons without spectral modification. We generate and verify photon-memory entanglement with a single-pair interference visibility of 88.1 [MATH] 10.6%. By exploiting the multimode capacity of the memory, we demonstrate high-dimensional photon-memory qudit entanglement spanning up to 63 temporal modes, leading to a maximum photon information efficiency of 5.1 Ebits per detected photon and a peak on-chip photon-memory entanglement rate of 5.6 kEbits s[MATH]. These results establish the first integrated platform for photon-memory entanglement generation and provide a scalable route toward chip-scale quantum repeaters and memory-enabled quantum networks operating over telecommunications infrastructure.
tldr: Demonstrates an integrated photonic platform for generating and storing entangled photons using dual silicon-carbide microring resonators, achieving high-dimensional qudit entanglement and record entanglement rates.
motivation: Scalable quantum networks require efficient generation, storage, and synchronization of entanglement between photonic qubits and quantum memories, but integrating spectrally matched sources and memories on a common platform remains challenging.
method: Two silicon-carbide microring resonators are integrated on a chip: one serves as an entangled photon-pair source via spontaneous four-wave mixing, and the other functions as a cavity-enhanced atomic-frequency-comb quantum memory using rare-earth ions. The resonators are intrinsically spectrally matched, enabling direct storage without spectral filtering.
result: Photon-memory entanglement is verified with 88.1% visibility, and high-dimensional qudit entanglement is demonstrated over up to 63 temporal modes, achieving a photon information efficiency of 5.1 Ebits per detected photon and a peak on-chip entanglement rate of 5.6 kEbits/s.
conclusion: This work establishes the first integrated platform for photon-memory entanglement generation, providing a scalable route toward chip-scale quantum repeaters and memory-enabled quantum networks operating over telecom infrastructure.

The memory resonator achieves an ensemble cooperativity of 1.9 and is intrinsically spectrally matched to the photon source, eliminating the need for external spectral filtering or conversion. The authors demonstrate photon-memory entanglement with a single-pair interference visibility of 88.1 ± 10.6%, and exploit the multimode capacity of the AFC memory to realize high-dimensional qudit entanglement spanning up to 63 temporal modes. title: Bit Flips Are Erasures In Dissipative Cat Qubits
authors: Filippo Ferrari, Joachim Cohen, Vincenzo Savona, Fabrizio Minganti
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous quantum error correction (QEC) stabilizes a logical manifold through dissipative events that emit into output channels, which are typically accessible to measurement. These signals are often discarded, and whether they contain useful information about logical failures remains generally unclear. Using quantum trajectories, we show that in dissipatively stabilized cat qubits bit flips are not silent logical errors: each flip is accompanied by a strong, time-localized photon burst from the dissipative buffer. Photon counting and homodyne monitoring can therefore herald the loss of logical information without interrupting the autonomous stabilization: bit flips in dissipative cat qubits are erasures. More broadly, our results show that the emitted signals of engineered reservoirs can act as built-in failure monitors for autonomous QEC, turning rare logical faults into erasures available to a decoder and reducing fault-tolerance overhead. To this end, we develop a general framework, based on past quantum states and number-resolved master equations, to quantify the detectability of such logical failures in autonomous QEC from the emitted signal.
tldr: This paper shows that bit flips in dissipative cat qubits are heralded by photon bursts, turning them into erasures detectable via output channel monitoring.
motivation: Autonomous quantum error correction often discards output signals; the authors investigate whether these signals contain information about logical failures, aiming to reduce fault-tolerance overhead.
method: Using quantum trajectories, past quantum states, and number-resolved master equations, they analyze the emitted signals from a dissipatively stabilized cat qubit.
result: Each bit flip is accompanied by a strong, time-localized photon burst, making bit flips detectable as erasures through photon counting or homodyne monitoring.
conclusion: Emitted signals from engineered reservoirs can serve as built-in failure monitors for autonomous QEC, converting rare logical faults into erasures and reducing overhead.

The paper develops a general framework based on past quantum states and number-resolved master equations to quantify the detectability of logical failures from emitted signals. This framework allows for the calculation of the probability of detecting a logical error given the measurement record, providing a rigorous way to assess the performance of such failure monitors. The results suggest that engineered reservoirs can act as built-in failure monitors for autonomous QEC, reducing fault-tolerance overhead by converting rare logical faults into erasures that can be handled by a decoder.

title: First Passage Time For An Underdamped Harmonic Oscillator And Application To The Power Of An Information Engine
authors: Aubin Archambault, Caroline Crauste-Thibierge, Alberto Imparato, Sergio Ciliberto, Ludovic Bellon
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The distribution of the first passage time [MATH] for the position [MATH] to overcome a threshold [MATH] is calculated in an underdamped harmonic oscillator. The proof combines several approaches based on the determination of the eigenvalues of the Kramers differential operator for the intermediate and long time regimes and on a Hamiltonian approximation for the short times. The theoretical predictions are in excellent agreement with the results of an experiment on an underdamped micro-cantilever. The knowledge of the [MATH] distribution opens the way to several applications, among them the precise estimation of the power of information engines, which we have also experimentally checked.
tldr: Calculates first passage time distribution for an underdamped harmonic oscillator and applies it to measure the power of an information engine.
motivation: First passage times are crucial for understanding stochastic processes in thermodynamics, and their distribution enables precise estimation of information engine power.
method: Combines eigenvalue analysis of the Kramers operator for intermediate/long times with a Hamiltonian approximation for short times, validated by micro-cantilever experiments.
result: Theoretical predictions match experimental data; the distribution is used to experimentally determine the power of an information engine.
conclusion: The derived first passage time distribution provides a practical tool for characterizing information engines and other stochastic thermodynamic systems.

abstract: ArXiv:2607.01473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires logical operations that manipulate encoded information while preserving quantum error-correction protection. In planar surface-code architectures, code deformation and lattice surgery provide a local, measurement-based route to such operations. Here we experimentally realize key elements of patch-based surface-code logical processing on a 107-qubit superconducting quantum processor. We first implement a reusable primitive layer comprising merge and split, patch expansion and shrinkage, and deformations mediated by domain walls and twist defects. We then compose these primitives to realize logical state routing, the logical controlled-NOT gate, and the single-qubit Hadamard and phase gates, which together form a Clifford-generating set. All operations are implemented on distance-three rotated surface-code patches with multi-round syndrome extraction and neural-network decoding, without post-selection. Our results advance superconducting surface-code experiments from protected logical memory to active, patch-based fault-tolerant logical operations.

title: Quantum Nonlocal Correlations Of Anomalous Weak Values
authors: Ron Cohen, Avshalom C. Elitzur, Eliahu Cohen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Violations of Bell inequalities are a hallmark of entanglement, with only entangled states capable of exceeding classical bounds in standard Bell tests. Here we analyze anomalous weak values of the CHSH operator in pre- and post-selected (PPS) quantum ensembles, treating them as generalized bounds on Bell-type nonlocal correlations in the presence of post-selection. Fixing the overlap between the pre- and post-selected states, we compare three scenarios: unrestricted boundary states, one separable boundary state, and both boundary states separable. For each case, we derive both the maximal weak value for a fixed Bell operator and the maximal bound obtained by further optimizing over all CHSH operators. Our results show that post-selection and entanglement are distinct operational resources: post-selection alone can enhance correlations, but entanglement is necessary to exceed the corresponding separable PPS bounds, and their combination yields the strongest attainable correlations. We further show that the enhancement beyond the separable bound closely tracks the concurrence of the states that optimize the bounds, identifying entanglement as the source of the additional correlation strength. Finally, we show that nonlocal weak values provide post-selected entanglement witnesses, and we give a constructive protocol that detects every pure two-qubit source state with nonzero concurrence in the ideal state-adapted setting, even in regimes where the corresponding standard CHSH entanglement test is inconclusive. In this state-adapted setting, we explicitly construct the post-selection and CHSH measurements that achieve the largest possible separation from the separable PPS bound. More broadly, our results motivate hybrid protocols that combine post-selection and entanglement, with possible applications to improved quantum sensing, weak-value amplification, and quantum information processing.
tldr: This paper analyzes anomalous weak values of the CHSH operator in pre- and post-selected ensembles, showing that post-selection and entanglement are distinct resources for nonlocal correlations.
motivation: To understand the interplay between post-selection and entanglement in generating nonlocal correlations beyond standard Bell tests.
method: The authors derive maximal weak values for CHSH operators under different constraints on pre- and post-selected states, and compare bounds for unrestricted, one separable, and both separable boundary states.
result: Post-selection alone can enhance correlations, but entanglement is necessary to exceed separable bounds; the enhancement tracks concurrence, and nonlocal weak values serve as entanglement witnesses.
conclusion: Hybrid protocols combining post-selection and entanglement can yield stronger correlations, with applications to quantum sensing and information processing.

title: Bayesian Monotone Metrics For Multiparameter Quantum Estimation
authors: Jianchao Zhang, Koichi Yamagata, Jun Suzuki
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bayesian quantum estimation offers a finite-data framework for quantum sensing and metrology, yet a unified geometric formulation for multiparameter Bayes risk has been lacking. We introduce Bayesian monotone metrics by evaluating Petz monotone metrics on the prior-averaged state, providing a Bayesian extension of the full class of statistically meaningful (CPTP) quantum metrics. This framework yields Bayesian quantities, including quantum posterior-mean operators and a quantum Bayesian dual Fisher-information matrix, and it leads to a systematic family of computable lower bounds on the Bayes risk. The resulting bounds naturally incorporate multiparameter measurement incompatibility and, for every monotone metric in the family, we prove a universal dominance over the corresponding quantum van Trees (Bayesian Cram\'er--Rao) bound. Moreover, we show that optimizing over all operator monotone functions collapses to a one-parameter subfamily, turning the tightest bound into a tractable optimization with a clear geometric interpretation. In representative examples, the optimized bounds are strictly tighter than the Bayesian SLD and RLD bounds. Our results establish Bayesian monotone metrics as a unifying information-geometric perspective on Bayesian quantum estimation, enabling systematic and computable performance limits in multiparameter settings.
tldr: This paper introduces Bayesian monotone metrics for multiparameter quantum estimation, providing a unified geometric framework and computable lower bounds on Bayes risk.
motivation: A unified geometric formulation for multiparameter Bayes risk in quantum estimation was lacking, and existing bounds like the quantum van Trees bound are not always tight.
method: The authors evaluate Petz monotone metrics on the prior-averaged state to define Bayesian monotone metrics, and derive Bayesian quantities including posterior-mean operators and a Bayesian dual Fisher-information matrix.
result: They prove that the resulting bounds universally dominate the quantum van Trees bound, and show that optimization over all operator monotone functions reduces to a one-parameter subfamily, yielding tractable and tighter bounds than Bayesian SLD and RLD bounds.
conclusion: Bayesian monotone metrics provide a unifying information-geometric perspective for Bayesian quantum estimation, enabling systematic and computable performance limits in multiparameter settings.

title: Extracting Work From Discrete Quantum Polytropic Processes
authors: Vishal Anand, Swarup Kumar Giri, Avijit Misra, Subhadip Mitra, Samyadeb Bhattacharya
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish an upper bound on extractable work for time-dependent, non-Markovian quantum heat engines operating with finite baths. This bound analytically isolates the distinct thermodynamic penalties arising from system-bath correlations, bath non-equilibrium, and residual interaction energy. Evaluating this framework operationally via a quantum polytropic cavity-optomechanical cycle, we demonstrate that maximal efficiency requires quasi-static operation to successfully harvest coherent, non-Markovian system-bath resonances. Conversely, optimising for maximum power enforces a strict finite-time regime. Under realistic hardware constraints, this acceleration necessitates larger discrete operational steps, where we expect Trotterisation errors to manifest as physical noise. Such noise would irreversibly suppress delicate quantum memory effects, forcing a collapse to the memoryless Markovian Otto limit. Coupled with the permanent energetic tax of switching finite-bath interactions, our results indicate that the exploitation of quantum memory resources and finite-power operation belong to different operational regimes.

motivation: To understand the thermodynamic penalties from system-bath correlations, bath non-equilibrium, and residual interaction energy in quantum heat engines, and to explore the trade-off between efficiency and power under realistic constraints.
method: Derives an analytical bound on extractable work using a framework that isolates distinct thermodynamic penalties, and evaluates it operationally via a quantum polytropic cavity-optomechanical cycle, considering Trotterisation errors and finite-bath interactions.
result: Maximal efficiency requires quasi-static operation to harvest coherent non-Markovian resonances, while maximum power enforces a finite-time regime where Trotterisation errors suppress quantum memory effects, collapsing to the Markovian Otto limit.
conclusion: Exploitation of quantum memory resources and finite-power operation belong to different operational regimes, with a permanent energetic tax from switching finite-bath interactions.

The authors derive a design rule for fault-tolerant packet sizes: for rotated surface codes of distance d, the maximum number of gates that can be packaged while preserving fault tolerance is ⌈d/2⌉ with a correlation-aware decoder, and ⌊d/2⌋ without. Simulations using PyMatching show that the standard MWPM decoder, built from the packet circuit's noise model, naturally corrects the correlated error. At network-to-local noise ratios γ = p_net/p_gate up to 100, the packet matches or surpasses the per-link sequential logical error rate (LER) at moderate-to-high γ, with the advantage growing with both γ and d, while reducing entanglement cost from n ebits to 1. Packetization wins when the network is the bottleneck (γ ≫ 1); at γ ≈ 1 the n−1 extra local fan-out gates offset the network savings. No custom decoder is required: the circuit-level noise model already encodes the correlation. These results enable noise-aware distributed circuit compilers to favor fan-out packetization without sacrificing fault tolerance.

They first analyze the error propagation in the fan-out circuit, showing that a single network fault leads to a weight-n Pauli error. Using the properties of rotated surface codes, they derive the maximum packet size n_max that preserves fault tolerance, considering both a naive decoder (which treats errors as independent) and a correlation-aware decoder (which accounts for the correlated error). The derivation relies on the fact that the correlated error has weight n, and the surface code can correct errors up to weight ⌊d/2⌋. For the correlation-aware decoder, the effective weight is reduced because the decoder can exploit the correlation structure. The simulation uses PyMatching to implement MWPM decoding on the circuit-level noise model of the packet circuit. The noise model includes local gate errors (p_gate) and network errors (p_net), with a fan-out structure that creates correlated errors. The logical error rate (LER) is compared between the packet circuit and sequential gate teleportation for various γ and d. The simulation results validate the analytical design rule and show the performance advantage of packetization.

For example, for distance-3 surface code, n_max = 2 (correlation-aware) or 1 (naive). For distance-5, n_max = 3 or 2. The simulation results show that at γ = 100 and d = 5, the packet circuit achieves LER ≈ 10^{-4}, while sequential teleportation achieves LER ≈ 10^{-3}, a factor of 10 improvement. At γ = 10, the packet LER is comparable to sequential, and at γ = 1, sequential outperforms packet due to the extra local fan-out gates. title: Monolithic Integration Of Piezo-Optomechanical Photonics And Cmos Electronics
authors: Matthew Zimmermann, Aileen Zhai, Andrew J. Leenheer, Julia Boyle, Mayank Mishra, Daniel Dominguez, Matthew Koppa, Wolf Jehle, Christopher Panuski, Mark Dong, Gerald Gilbert, Dirk Englund, Matt Eichenfield
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Next-generation photonic architectures for AI, sensing, and quantum computing require thousands to millions of reprogrammable photonic devices on a chip[1]. The monolithic integration of Electronically-backed Photonic Integrated Circuits (EPICs) allows for very high density electrical interconnection and electronic drivers that can scale with photonics. Piezo-optomechanical photonic integrated circuits (POMPICs) offer low power consumption, high speed modulation, cryogenic compatibility and broadband optical transparency from ultraviolet to infrared wavelengths[2,3], but have not been demonstrated with monolithically integrated CMOS electronics. Here, we show a fully monolithic, all-CMOS fabricated platform for POMPICs co-fabricated with commercial control electronics. 200 millimeter photonic wafers are constructed directly on completed CMOS driver wafers by back-end-of-line processing, connecting integrated piezoelectric actuators under broadband silicon nitride waveguides to a high-density digital backplane comprising >2 million electrical connections per die with 6.4x6.4 micron electrode pitch. We introduce segmented POMPIC components as Photonic Digital-to-Analog converters (PDACs) that convert low-voltage digital electronic signals to multi-bit analog optical phase and amplitude modulation, and we demonstrate parallel control of optical phase shifters, Mach-Zehnder interferometers, optical routing trees, and tunable ring resonators using a standard HDMI interface to program CMOS electronics. We test multiple reticles and perform electronic and photonic characterization across the entire wafer to establish uniformity and yield, demonstrating wafer-scale integration of POMPICs on an electronic backplane and enabling dense, scalable electronic control of piezo-optomechanical circuits.
tldr: This paper demonstrates the monolithic integration of piezo-optomechanical photonic integrated circuits with CMOS electronics on a 200 mm wafer, enabling dense, scalable electronic control of photonic devices.
motivation: Next-generation photonic architectures for AI, sensing, and quantum computing require thousands to millions of reprogrammable photonic devices on a chip, but previous piezo-optomechanical platforms lacked monolithic CMOS integration.
method: The authors fabricate photonic wafers directly on completed CMOS driver wafers using back-end-of-line processing, connecting piezoelectric actuators under silicon nitride waveguides to a high-density digital backplane with over 2 million electrical connections per die.
result: They demonstrate parallel control of optical phase shifters, Mach-Zehnder interferometers, optical routing trees, and tunable ring resonators using a standard HDMI interface, and characterize uniformity and yield across the wafer.
conclusion: This work establishes a scalable platform for dense electronic control of piezo-optomechanical circuits, which is relevant for quantum networking and hybrid quantum systems.

title: An Information-Theoretic Principle For Optimal Quantum Encoding: Tight Frames And Equiangular Ensembles
authors: Shuixin Xiao Farhad Farokhi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01564v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optimal encoding of classical data for quantum-assisted statistical inference is investigated from an information-theoretic perspective. We prove that the accuracy of any quantum-computing inference procedure is upper bounded by the maximal quantum leakage from the classical data through its quantum encoding, establishing leakage as a universal, task-agnostic quality measure for encoders. This demonstrates that the maximal quantum leakage is a universal measure of the quality of the encoding strategy for statistical inference as it only depends on the quantum encoding of the data and not the inference task itself. The optimal universal encoding strategy, i.e., an encoding strategy that maximizes the maximal quantum leakage, is proved to be attained by pure states. When there are enough qubits, basis encoding is proved to be universally optimal. However, when the dimension of the system is small, phase encoding is optimal. For the latter, any tight frame, any ensemble whose average state is the maximally mixed state, is in fact optimal. Within tight frames, equiangular tight frames (ETFs) are distinguished as the uniquely symmetric optimal encodings, i.e., they saturate the Welch lower bound on pairwise overlaps and possess a self-referential optimal measurement. Prominent special cases are the qubit trine, the regular simplex, and symmetric informationally complete positive operator-valued measures (SIC-POVMs), for which the ETF structure and explicit codeword constructions are provided. Numerical examples are presented to validate the theoretical predictions.
tldr: This paper proves that maximal quantum leakage is a universal, task-agnostic quality measure for quantum encodings in statistical inference, and identifies optimal encodings as tight frames, with equiangular tight frames as uniquely symmetric optimal encodings.
motivation: To find an optimal encoding strategy for classical data into quantum states that maximizes the accuracy of any subsequent quantum-assisted inference procedure, independent of the specific inference task.
method: The authors derive an upper bound on inference accuracy in terms of maximal quantum leakage, then characterize encodings that maximize this leakage, showing that pure states are optimal and that tight frames (including equiangular tight frames) achieve optimality under dimension constraints.
result: Maximal quantum leakage is a universal quality measure; optimal encodings are pure states; basis encoding is optimal when enough qubits are available, otherwise phase encoding; any tight frame is optimal, and equiangular tight frames (e.g., SIC-POVMs) are uniquely symmetric optimal encodings.
conclusion: The work provides a principled information-theoretic framework for designing quantum encodings for inference, with explicit constructions and numerical validation.

title: $r$-deformed $\alpha$-$z$-R\'enyi Relative Entropy
authors: Srikrishna Maity, Shigeru Furuichi, Supriyo Dutta
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01805v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this article, we consider the [MATH]-logarithm for defining three-parameter family of R\'{e}nyi relative entropies that are generalization of the [MATH]-[MATH]-R\'{e}nyi relative entropies. We expose the range of parameters [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH] for which the data processing inequality holds. We also establish that [MATH]-deformed [MATH]-[MATH]-R\'{e}nyi relative entropy is an upper bound of the Tsallis relative entropy. Now, we have two upper bounds of the Tsallis relative entropy, which are [MATH]-deformed [MATH]-[MATH]-R\'{e}nyi relative entropy and the other one, which is discussed in literature. We investigate the order relationship between these two upper bounds of the Tsallis relative entropy. We observe that our new upper bound is more tighter when applicable to the density operators.

The paper then compares these two upper bounds and demonstrates that the new bound is tighter when applied to density operators, offering a more refined estimate.

title: Shallow Unitary Circuits For Kramers-Wannier Dualities

abstract: ArXiv:2607.01624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum Kramers-Wannier (KW) duality is a fundamental transformation mapping short-range entangled (SRE) states to long-range entangled (LRE) states. title: One-Body Purity, Non-Gaussianity, And Entanglement In Interacting Integrable Models
authors: Rafa{\l} \'swi\k{e}tek, Maksymilian Kliczkowski, Lev Vidmar, Marcos Rigol
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When describing entanglement in typical midspectrum eigenstates of many-body lattice Hamiltonians, two paradigms have emerged that capture the behavior observed in integrable and nonintegrable systems, Haar-random fermionic Gaussian states and Haar-random pure states, respectively. Remarkably, the former capture the behavior of interacting integrable systems, whose eigenstates are non-Gaussian. We argue that the paradigm that captures both the entanglement properties and the lack of Gaussianity in integrable systems is that of random superpositions of polynomially many Gaussian states. In contrast, eigenstates of nonintegrable systems are consistent with being described by random superpositions of exponentially many Gaussian states. We gain this understanding by comparing analytical and numerical results for the one-body purity, the non-Gaussianity, and the entanglement entropy of the random superpositions and the Hamiltonian eigenstates.

result: Eigenstates of integrable systems are consistent with random superpositions of polynomially many Gaussian states, while nonintegrable ones require exponentially many.
conclusion: The paradigm of random superpositions of Gaussian states unifies entanglement and non-Gaussianity in integrable systems, providing a new framework for understanding their eigenstate structure.

title: Quantum Trajectory Entanglement In Seeded Boundary Time Crystals
authors: Fernando Iemini Mohammad Jafari
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the entanglement dynamics along quantum trajectories during the seeding of time-crystalline order in a boundary time crystal (BTC). Specifically, how entanglement spreads among different spin ensembles when a BTC attempts to seed its time-crystalline behavior onto otherwise static spin ensembles, through a collective dissipative channel. In the seeded BTC phase, the steady-state entanglement entropy between the ensembles grows with system size [MATH], accompanied by macroscopic fluctuations along the trajectories. In contrast, in the non-seeded static phase, both the steady-state entanglement and its fluctuations decay exponentially with [MATH]. The model thus features a measurement-induced phase transition (MIPT) driven by the seeding mechanism. Furthermore, these findings establish dissipative seeding as a powerful mechanism for controlling quantum correlations in open many-body systems, with direct experimental relevance to this class of model without a postselection barrier.

title: Noisy Quantum Circuit Simulation With The Tensor Jump Method
authors: Maximilian Fr\"ohlich, Aaron Sander, Martin Eigel, Robert Wille, Michael Hinterm\"uller
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01323v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical simulation of noisy quantum circuits is essential for validating algorithms, benchmarking hardware, and assessing error-mitigation strategies, but remains limited by the exponential cost of density-matrix methods and the high variance of standard trajectory sampling. We introduce a variance-aware tensor network framework that combines the tensor jump method with local TDVP gate evolution on matrix product states and sparse Pauli-Lindblad hardware noise models. Gates are applied as short variational evolutions on the MPS manifold, while noise is sampled per circuit window from Pauli-Lindblad jump sets with state-independent hazards and dissipative contractions that reduce to irrelevant global factors after renormalization. The method supports correlated multi-qubit Lindblad noise consistent with hardware connectivity, including long-range operators on non-adjacent qubits, enabling direct simulation of crosstalk and other connectivity-induced errors beyond local noise models. We develop two unbiased variance-aware unravelings. An analog unitary-mixture unraveling matches the Lindblad generator exactly under symmetric Gaussian or two-point angle laws, while a projector-jump unraveling yields state-independent hazards and closed-form variance laws. Both retain the standard 1/sqrt(N) Monte Carlo convergence but with reduced prefactors. Empirically, projector sampling strongly reduces trajectory variance and bond-dimension growth across many circuit architectures, whereas analog sampling is most effective at weak noise. We demonstrate accurate, scalable noisy-circuit simulation on a 25-qubit noisy XY quench and IBM's 127-qubit kicked-Ising benchmark with long-range depolarizing noise, achieving reduced Monte Carlo variance and favorable MPS bond-dimension growth compared with standard Kraus-insertion baselines.

title: Controlling Waiting Time Statistics In Monitored Collective Spins: Mitigating Detector's Resolution Barrier In Measurement-Induced Phase Transitions
authors: Fernando Iemini Tanbir Islam
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In collective dissipative spin systems, the postselection barrier can be partially mitigated; however, a further obstacle may be posed by the finite temporal resolution of detectors. In this work, we investigate how initial-state inhomogeneities can control waiting-time statistics between quantum jumps, thereby mitigating the detector-resolution problem. We consider a collectively monitored spin model with a boundary time-crystalline phase, introducing inhomogeneity by partitioning the ensemble into two subsystems rotated by an angle [MATH]. We find that the measurement-induced phase transition survives under inhomogeneities, with different entanglement scaling regimes. The waiting time increases with [MATH], scaling as [MATH] but with a prefactor strongly enhanced by orders of magnitude, and in the anti-aligned limit [MATH] it remains finite, fully resolving the resolution barrier. This mitigation, however, comes at a cost: the entanglement saturation time becomes significantly longer, partially reintroducing the postselection barrier. Our results highlight a trade-off between detector resolution and postselection overhead, with direct implications for the experimental observation of measurement-induced phenomena.

title: First Passage Time Distribution In Underdamped Harmonic Oscillators
authors: Aubin Archambault, Caroline Crauste-Thibierge, Alberto Imparato, Sergio Ciliberto, Ludovic Bellon
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive the distribution of the first passage time [MATH] for the position [MATH] of an underdamped harmonic oscillator to overcome a threshold [MATH]. As the [MATH] distribution depends on the oscillator quality factor [MATH] different approaches are used. At very large quality factor ([MATH]) and intermediate and long [MATH] the proof is based on an energy diffusion model, whereas at medium quality factor ([MATH]) the proof is based on the study of the eigenvalues of the Kramers linear differential operator with absorbing boundary conditions. For all [MATH] and short [MATH] we use a Hamiltonian approximation. The theoretical predictions are in excellent agreement with direct numerical simulations of underdamped oscillator dynamics. Finally we show that the mean of the trajectories ending at [MATH] presents a particular shape driven by a specific noise pattern.
tldr: Derives the first passage time distribution for an underdamped harmonic oscillator using energy diffusion, Kramers operator, and Hamiltonian approximation.
motivation: First passage time is a key quantity in stochastic processes and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, relevant to understanding fluctuations in small systems.
method: Analytical derivations using energy diffusion model for high quality factor, eigenvalue analysis of Kramers operator for medium quality factor, and Hamiltonian approximation for short times.
result: Theoretical predictions match numerical simulations; mean trajectories exhibit a specific shape driven by noise.
conclusion: Provides a comprehensive analytical framework for first passage times in underdamped oscillators, useful for thermodynamic and stochastic analyses.

Additionally, the paper shows that the mean trajectory conditioned on the first passage time exhibits a specific shape driven by a particular noise pattern.

title: Symmetry Conservation With Trotterization And Quantum Phase Estimation
authors: Edith Leal-S\'anchez, Fanny Vain, Jong-Kwon Ha, Ryan J. Macdonell
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum algorithms for quantum chemistry and other many-body fermionic systems work by expressing the Hamiltonian in a basis of qubits and fragmenting the Hamiltonian into a sum of products of Pauli operators whose exponentials are easily encoded on a quantum device. Applying the product of exponentials, known as Trotterization, leads to an error associated with the non-commutativity of operators. This error can lead to breaking the symmetries of the Hamiltonian because the fragments are not symmetry conserving in general. Nonetheless, many algorithms for time evolution rely on Trotterization, including time evolution and quantum phase estimation. We show that we can express the Hamiltonian in terms of Hermitian excitation operators which map to sums of commuting Pauli strings for any encoding and conserve symmetries corresponding to Abelian groups of symmetry operators. Symmetries corresponding to non-Abelian groups, on the other hand, are not fully conserved by Trotterized Hermitian excitation operators, so we developed ``operator kirigami'' to cut the sum of non-commuting operators by orthogonal projection and to fold terms together using unitary rotations. We tested pools of operators for small molecules and basis sets, and found that electron number and spin symmetry conserving pools led to greater errors that decreased for larger molecules and were negated with second-order Trotterization. Our work shows the potential for testing quantum computing algorithms on classical computers by adapting tools used in electronic structure theory with conserved symmetries.
tldr: This paper introduces symmetry-conserving Trotterization methods for quantum phase estimation, using Hermitian excitation operators and 'operator kirigami' to preserve Abelian and partially non-Abelian symmetries.
motivation: Trotterization in quantum algorithms often breaks Hamiltonian symmetries, leading to errors; preserving symmetries is crucial for accurate quantum chemistry simulations.
method: The authors express the Hamiltonian in terms of Hermitian excitation operators that map to commuting Pauli strings, conserving Abelian symmetries. For non-Abelian symmetries, they develop 'operator kirigami' using orthogonal projection and unitary rotations to fold non-commuting terms.
result: Tests on small molecules show that symmetry-conserving pools increase error for small systems but errors decrease for larger molecules and are mitigated by second-order Trotterization.
conclusion: The work demonstrates the potential of testing quantum algorithms on classical computers by adapting electronic structure tools with conserved symmetries.

This is achieved by finding a unitary that diagonalizes the non-commuting part. The approach is tested on small molecules (e.g., H2, LiH) using various basis sets, comparing Trotter errors for symmetry-conserving and non-conserving operator pools. The analysis includes first- and second-order Trotterization.

title: A Validation Framework For Quantum Simulation Of Spin Dynamics Against Inelastic Neutron Scattering And Classical Simulation
authors: Gilles Buchs, Elaine Wong, Anshumitra Baul, Kathleen E. Hamilton, Arnab Banerjee, Stephan Eidenbenz, G\'abor B. Hal\'asz, Keerthi Kumaran, Thomas Maier, Thomas Naughton III, Elijah Pelofske, Vincent Russo, Allen Scheie, Yigit Subasi, D. Alan Tennant, Akram Touil, Travis S. Humble, Andrew T. Sornborger
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantitative validation of quantum simulations of dynamical spin response remains challenging because experiment, classical simulation, and quantum simulation do not produce the same native observables. This problem has become increasingly important as quantum simulation protocols for dynamical response have progressed from theory to hardware-level benchmarking against neutron-scattering data, while the longer term goal is validation in regimes that may eventually become classically intractable, including in future fault-tolerant implementations. Here, we develop a cross-pipeline validation framework for quantum simulation, using inelastic neutron scattering and classical many-body simulation as complementary experimental and computational anchors, based on explicit forward and inverse observable maps, covariance- or resampling-based uncertainty propagation, robustness tests for structured distortion, and a hierarchy of complementary metric families. The framework distinguishes stochastic uncertainty from robustness-induced distortion, carries both explicitly through the comparison chain, and uses the resulting metric-level uncertainty and distortion information to support layered validation at the pipeline, solver, and model levels. We also introduce actuator-aware feedback logic aimed at improving agreement without obscuring the physical origin of any remaining mismatch. We close by outlining future extensions of this methodology, including upstream uncertainty and distortion modeling, adaptive feedback, asymmetric validation beyond full classical benchmarking, fault-tolerant workflows, and community infrastructure for reproducible validation.
tldr: A cross-pipeline validation framework for quantum simulation of spin dynamics using inelastic neutron scattering and classical simulation as anchors.
motivation: Quantitative validation of quantum simulations of dynamical spin response is challenging because experiment, classical simulation, and quantum simulation produce different native observables.
method: The framework uses explicit forward and inverse observable maps, covariance- or resampling-based uncertainty propagation, robustness tests for structured distortion, and a hierarchy of complementary metric families.
result: The framework distinguishes stochastic uncertainty from robustness-induced distortion and supports layered validation at pipeline, solver, and model levels.
conclusion: The methodology enables validation in regimes that may become classically intractable, with future extensions to fault-tolerant workflows.

title: Noise Suppression Via Pulsed All-Optical Magnetometry With Nitrogen-Vacancy Ensembles
authors: Xiechen Zheng, Jeyson T\'amara-Isaza, John W. Blanchard, Ronald L. Walsworth
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: All-optical (AO) microwave-free magnetometry using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond simplifies experimental design and broadens sample compatibility. While continuous-wave (cw) detection of AO photoluminescence (PL) changes is commonly employed, its performance is susceptible to systematic fluctuations such as optical intensity noise. To address these challenges, we introduce a pulsed AO protocol that employs two PL measurements within an optical pulse to suppress common-mode noise. At near-zero magnetic field, we experimentally demonstrate that the pulsed AO protocol resolves AO-PL contrast features arising from NV-NV cross-relaxation, achieving up to 10[MATH] improvement in the low-frequency noise floor compared to conventional cw AO techniques. We further investigate the dependence of AO-PL contrast on PL readout timing and the dark time duration [MATH] between optical pulses, with the optimal [MATH] varying based on NV concentrations. These findings provide insights into optimizing NV-diamond samples for effective AO operation across diverse applications.
tldr: This paper introduces a pulsed all-optical magnetometry protocol using NV ensembles to suppress low-frequency noise, achieving up to 10x improvement in noise floor.
motivation: Continuous-wave all-optical magnetometry with NV centers suffers from systematic noise like optical intensity fluctuations, limiting sensitivity.
method: A pulsed protocol with two photoluminescence measurements within an optical pulse is used to cancel common-mode noise, and the dependence on readout timing and dark time is studied.
result: The pulsed protocol resolves AO-PL contrast features from NV-NV cross-relaxation and improves the low-frequency noise floor by up to 10x compared to cw methods.
conclusion: The pulsed AO technique offers a simple and effective way to enhance NV magnetometry performance, with optimal parameters depending on NV concentration.

title: Chiral Interaction Enhanced Magnon Bundle Emission
authors: Zhicai Chen, Deyi Kong, Chengdeng Gou, Xiangming Hu, Fei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we suggest a chiral interaction scheme to enhance magnon bundle emission by placing a qubit and a magnon into a cascaded-cavity setup, respectively. It is found that the unidirectional interaction prolongs the lifetime of the target excited state, thereby suppressing the magnon re-excitation and promoting both the average purity and number of two-magnon bundles. Consequently, the chiral interaction not only offers directional control but also improves the quality of the multi-magnon source, which may find potential applications in quantum information processing.
tldr: A chiral interaction scheme enhances magnon bundle emission by suppressing re-excitation, improving multi-magnon source quality.
motivation: Multi-magnon sources are important for quantum information processing, but existing schemes suffer from re-excitation that degrades purity and number.
method: Place a qubit and a magnon in a cascaded-cavity setup with unidirectional (chiral) coupling to prolong the target excited state lifetime.
result: The chiral interaction suppresses magnon re-excitation, increasing both the average purity and number of two-magnon bundles.
conclusion: Chiral interaction provides directional control and improves multi-magnon source quality, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

This leads to improved purity and number of two-magnon bundles compared to conventional bidirectional coupling. The scheme offers directional control and enhances the quality of multi-magnon sources, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Performance Of A Two-mode Coherent Superposed Channel In Continuous-variable Quantum Teleportation
authors: Arpita Chatterjee Deepak
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01786v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Glauber's coherent state is denoted by [MATH] and its two-mode extension is represented by [MATH]. In this work, we introduce a two-mode superposition operator [MATH], whose action on the two-mode coherent state produces the two-mode coherent superposed quantum state [MATH]. We investigate the nonclassicality and quantum non-Gaussianity of this state by means of the Wigner distribution and Wigner logarithmic negativity. Once its intrinsic nonclassical and non-Gaussian structure is established, the state is employed as the entangled resource in the Braunstein-Kimble continuous-variable (CV) teleportation protocol. We compute the ideal teleportation fidelity for coherent and squeezed inputs and analyze how the strengths of nonclassicality and non-Gaussianity influence the teleportation efficiency. Our results identify specific parameter regimes where enhanced non-Gaussian features or increased nonclassicality enable fidelities beyond the classical threshold, thereby revealing the operational significance of engineered two-mode quantum states in CV quantum information processing.

motivation: To explore how engineered nonclassical and non-Gaussian states can improve the fidelity of continuous-variable quantum teleportation beyond classical limits.
method: The authors define a two-mode superposition operator acting on coherent states, analyze nonclassicality via Wigner distribution and Wigner logarithmic negativity, and compute teleportation fidelity for coherent and squeezed inputs.
result: Specific parameter regimes are identified where enhanced non-Gaussian features or increased nonclassicality enable fidelities exceeding the classical threshold.
conclusion: Engineered two-mode quantum states have operational significance for improving continuous-variable quantum information processing tasks like teleportation.

authors: Changpeng Shao Yuxin Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Block encodings are a central primitive in quantum algorithms, but standard constructions typically require logarithmic ancilla overhead and complicated controlled operations. Using higher-order Trotterization, we obtain an [MATH]-approximate block encoding of [MATH] with only one ancilla qubit and circuit depth [MATH] where [MATH]. Using multiproduct formulas, we obtain circuit depth [MATH], at the cost of [MATH] ancilla qubits. Our constructions provide alternatives to the standard LCU framework, with a focus on reducing the number of ancilla qubits while maintaining (near-)optimal circuit depth.

title: A Quantum Model Of Opinion Dynamics On Networks
authors: Weiqi Chu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01452v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical models of opinion dynamics represent individual opinions as scalar or vector values governed by the classical probability theory, either as deterministic quantities or random variables. This framework does not account for empirically observed phenomena such as cognitive ambivalence (where an individual simultaneously holds conflicting views) and order effects (where survey responses depend on the order in which questions are asked). We propose a quantum model of opinion dynamics in which each agent's cognitive state is represented by a density matrix that encodes both the expressed opinion and cognitive ambivalence. Survey questions become non-commuting self-adjoint operators, which provides a principled explanation for order effects. Our model also identifies quantities without classical counterparts, including quantum coherence and pairwise opinion covariances. Under a product state approximation, the quantum model reduces to the classical Friedkin--Johnsen opinion model. We test the framework on synthetic and real-world networks and observe that pairwise correlations follow network-dependent transient dynamics but converge to the same steady state regardless of the network, and that quantum coherence decays exponentially at a rate independent of the network.
tldr: A quantum model of opinion dynamics using density matrices and non-commuting observables to capture cognitive ambivalence and order effects.
motivation: Classical opinion models fail to explain cognitive ambivalence and order effects; a quantum framework can capture these phenomena.
method: Each agent's cognitive state is represented by a density matrix; survey questions are non-commuting operators; dynamics are modeled via quantum channels.
result: The model reduces to classical Friedkin-Johnsen under product state approximation; pairwise correlations converge to same steady state regardless of network; quantum coherence decays exponentially at a network-independent rate.
conclusion: Quantum probability offers a principled way to model opinion dynamics with richer structure than classical models.

title: Structured Factorization Approaches For Quantum State Tomography
authors: Zhen Qin, Joseph M. Lukens, Brian T. Kirby, Zhihui Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Since the complexity of quantum state tomography (QST) scales exponentially with system size, exploiting priors such as low-rankness, tensor-network structures, and neural-network representations is essential for scalable QST in terms of sample complexity and parameter complexity. In this paper, we introduce a unified framework, termed structured factorization, that builds on BurerMonteiro-type factorization by parametrizing the density matrix as [MATH], where the factor [MATH] is constrained to belong to a structured model class. This factorization guarantees physical validity by construction while allowing a broad range of structural priors to be incorporated directly through the choice of the factor space, ranging from the generic Cholesky decomposition to low-rank matrices, matrix product operators, and neural density operators based on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures. Building on this structured factorization framework, we formulate QST as an optimization problem over the factor space from measurement data. We first develop a unified statistical analysis of the sample complexity of least-squares estimation for a broad class of structured quantum states. We then propose a projected gradient descent method that operates directly on the factor space and accommodates a wide range of structural parametrizations and reconstruction objectives. To further exploit the geometry of the maximum-likelihood estimation formulation and the constraints on the factors, we derive a power method that yields a step-size-free algorithm with fast convergence, recovering Covers method as a special case when the factor is unconstrained.
tldr: A unified framework for quantum state tomography using structured factorization that incorporates low-rank, tensor-network, and neural-network priors.
motivation: Quantum state tomography is exponentially costly; exploiting structural priors is essential for scalability.
method: Parametrizes the density matrix as a product of a factor matrix and its conjugate, where the factor is constrained to a structured model class (e.g., low-rank, matrix product operator, neural network).
result: Provides sample complexity analysis and proposes projected gradient descent and a power method for optimization.
conclusion: The framework unifies many existing QST approaches and enables efficient reconstruction with various structural priors.

title: Ravines In Quantum Cost Landscapes: Opportunities For Improved Vqa Predictions
authors: Jo\~ao F. Bravo Felix J. Beckmann
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The geometric and topological structure of quantum cost landscapes (QCLs) governs the optimization and thus the predictive power of variational quantum algorithms (VQAs). We systematically analyze ravines - low-cost paths connecting local minima - using an adapted version of the nudged elastic band (NEB) algorithm, a method originating from theoretical chemistry. By training quantum neural networks (QNNs) to classify the concentratable entanglement of quantum states, we apply the NEB algorithm and numerically identify ravine structures in QCLs of hardware-efficient ansatzes. Beyond visualizing these ravines, we construct an ensemble prediction framework by averaging predictions from QNNs parameterized along the low-cost NEB path. We introduce a resource-light pre-training metric which quantifies local-prediction variability and serves as a strong performance indicator for VQAs, even beyond the scope of this study. When base classifiers are drawn from circuit and weight initializations exhibiting high local-prediction variability, the quantum-based NEB ensembles outperform both classical and naive quantum alternatives. Moreover, a complexity analysis shows that leveraging the ravine-like structure of QCLs with the QNN NEB approach substantially reduces computational costs compared to naive QNN ensembling. A depth and qubit scaling analysis indicates that ravines persist across both scalings, and that, despite the expected growth in resource requirements with the qubit scaling, the NEB approach also accelerates convergence over the naive alternative.
tldr: This paper analyzes ravines (low-cost paths between local minima) in quantum cost landscapes of variational quantum algorithms using a nudged elastic band method, and proposes an ensemble prediction framework to improve VQA performance.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms suffer from optimization challenges due to the structure of quantum cost landscapes; understanding and exploiting ravines can improve predictive power and reduce computational costs.
method: The authors adapt the nudged elastic band algorithm from chemistry to identify ravine structures in quantum cost landscapes of hardware-efficient ansatzes, and construct an ensemble of quantum neural networks along the low-cost path.
result: The quantum-based NEB ensembles outperform classical and naive quantum alternatives when base classifiers exhibit high local-prediction variability, and the approach reduces computational costs compared to naive ensembling.
conclusion: Ravines persist across depth and qubit scaling, and the NEB approach accelerates convergence, offering a resource-light pre-training metric for VQAs.

title: High-Precision Calibration Workflow Achieves Above $99.9\%$ Cz Gate Fidelity On A Scalable Superconducting Processor
authors: Huili Zhang, Meiling Li, Shuang Yang, Yaqing Feng, Yulong Li, Cheng Chen, Pei Liu, Guangming Xue, Haifeng Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-fidelity universal two-qubit gates are critical for building fault-tolerant quantum computers. In scalable superconducting processors, shortened coherence times introduce more incoherent errors in gate operations. With a constrained error budget, there is reduced tolerance for coherent errors stemming from parameter deviations. In this work, we develop a closed-loop workflow to enhance the CZ gate calibration precision. Utilizing the echoed leakage error amplification (ELEA) and the repurposed context-aware fidelity estimation (CAFE) circuits, we suppress the population leakage to non-computational states, and, for the first time, demonstrate a CZ gate fidelity exceeding [MATH] on an 84-qubit processor, with coherent error suppressed to [MATH]. Meanwhile, we obtain a median fidelity of [MATH] among 72 CZ gates, demonstrating that the workflow can be generalized to the calibration of parallel CZ gates. Finally, we realize automated calibration and observe enhanced stability of the CZ gate throughout 9-hour comparative monitoring experiments. Our results, realized on a completely domestic platform, establish an efficient and automated route to quantum computation with superconducting quantum systems.

title: Lamb Shift Of A Static Atom Facing A Rotating Surface
authors: C\'esar D. Fosco, Fernando C. Lombardo, Francisco D. Mazzitelli
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how the Lamb shift of a static atom is modified when a nearby planar body rotates rigidly about its normal while the atom is held at a fixed distance [MATH]. We derive a general formula for the shift in terms of the angularly Doppler-shifted reflection coefficients of the surface, valid for any axially symmetric planar material. Expanding the result to second order in the angular velocity [MATH], we identify two independent contributions associated with the orbital and spin components of the electromagnetic angular momentum. The orbital contribution, proportional to [MATH], reproduces locally the Lamb shift induced by a surface translating at the tangential velocity [MATH], whereas the spin contribution, proportional to [MATH], originates from the rotational Doppler shift of the photon helicity and survives even on the rotation axis. We first illustrate the formalism using a graphene sheet and then apply it to finite-thickness Drude and plasma conductors and to doped semiconductors. title: Structure-Aware Compilation For Scalable Neutral-Atom Quantum Computing
authors: Dekuan Dong, Fengyu Zou, Hengzhun Chen, Guorui Zhu, Yingzhou Li
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the compilation of structured quantum gate families on two-dimensional neutral-atom arrays, aiming to reduce addressing and transport overhead under realistic hardware constraints. For single-qubit gates, we exploit the algebraic structures of gate families at the matrix level, enabling efficient rank-one decompositions over appropriate algebraic structures and thereby reducing the number of addressing layers. For controlled-Z (C-Z) gates, we formulate the transport scheduling problem using graph-theoretic models, leading to efficient compilation algorithms under realistic transport constraints. We provide provable performance guarantees for the proposed methods and validate them through extensive numerical experiments. Across representative single-qubit gate families, our methods reduce the number of addressing layers by up to a factor of two compared with na\"ive row- or column-wise implementations. For C-Z gates, our scheduling strategy reduces the required number of atom transport operations by approximately 50\%. When applied to QAOA circuits for MaxCut, the proposed framework reduces transport cost by more than 30\% on average. These results show that the physical constraints of neutral-atom hardware can be converted into algebraic and graph-theoretic structure, turning a hardware-level scheduling bottleneck into tractable decomposition and coloring problems.

method: For single-qubit gates, they use rank-one decompositions over algebraic structures to reduce addressing layers. For C-Z gates, they formulate transport scheduling as a graph coloring problem and provide provable performance guarantees.

title: Generalized Extended Codes With Applications In Entanglement-Assisted Qubit And Qutrit Codes
authors: Yang Li, Martianus Frederic Ezerman, Shitao Li, San Ling, Zhonghua Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that any generalized extended code is monomially equivalent to the Hermitian dual of a code which is closely related to a second kind of extended code of [MATH]. We then characterize the Hermitian hull and Hermitian dual distance of [MATH] in terms of the position of [MATH] relative to [MATH] and the interaction between [MATH] and the minimum weight codewords of [MATH], respectively. title: Decohered Toric Code Under Quantum Damping Noise And Its Mapping To A Classical Spin Model
authors: Nihar Ranjan Dash, Sanjoy Dutta, R. Srikanth, Subhashish Banerjee
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate properties of toric codes under realistic damping error channels, which include squeezing, thermal and non-Markovian effects. First, we map the decohered toric code under the generalized amplitude-damping (GAD) and the squeezed generalized amplitude-damping (SGAD) channels to the statistical-mechanical models using the double Hilbert-space formalism. Second, we map the action of the GAD and SGAD channels on the toric code to stochastic Pauli-type errors via Pauli twirling, yielding asymmetric depolarizing channels, and obtain the logical failure probabilities as a function of temperature and squeezing. In both cases, we relate the channel parameters of the GAD and SGAD channels to the spin-coupling constants of the statistical-mechanical model.
tldr: This paper maps decohered toric codes under generalized amplitude-damping noise to classical spin models and analyzes logical failure probabilities.
motivation: Understanding the performance of topological quantum error-correcting codes under realistic noise models is crucial for practical quantum computing.
method: The authors use the double Hilbert-space formalism and Pauli twirling to map the decohered toric code under GAD and SGAD channels to statistical-mechanical models and asymmetric depolarizing channels.
result: They derive logical failure probabilities as functions of temperature and squeezing, and relate channel parameters to spin-coupling constants.
conclusion: The mapping provides a framework to analyze toric codes under non-Markovian and squeezed noise, but the results are incremental and not directly advancing core quantum information theory.

title: Luci On Ibm Hardware: Error Suppression With Almost Half Syndrome Density
authors: Younghun Kim, Spiro Gicev, Martin Sevior, Muhammad Usman
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-lived logical qubits are essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, the practical performance of traditional error correction protocols relies on performing specific syndrome circuits, causing vulnerability to hardware defects and imposing rigid connectivity constraints. Recent theoretical findings have proposed that flexible subroutine circuits within the LUCI framework can maintain space-time distance in the presence of isolated or broken components, albeit at the expense of temporal distance. However, these approaches have solely targeted defect avoidance and have not yet been demonstrated to suppress errors with reduced temporal distances on physical hardware. In this work, we propose a reset-free scenario for the LUCI framework and experimentally benchmark it on IBM quantum hardware. By asymmetrically scaling the [MATH] or [MATH] distance, we compare our reset-free approach against the standard surface code and successfully demonstrate error suppression ratios for targeted logical Pauli errors. Remarkably, despite a nearly halved syndrome density in time, which requires two subroutine rounds for full syndrome extraction, the LUCI framework remains competitive with the rotated surface code implementation. In the LUCI framework, we observe error suppression of [MATH] for logical [MATH] errors and [MATH] for logical [MATH] errors, whereas the standard approach yields [MATH] and [MATH], respectively. These results demonstrate that dynamic codes outperform standard methods by avoiding highly noisy components, even without physical defects, while preserving logical boundaries. Our findings challenge the conventional dependency on static fault-tolerant architectures by verifying the feasibility and efficacy of the LUCI framework on physical hardware and pave the way for hybrid, hardware-compatible code designs in quantum computing.

motivation: Long-lived logical qubits are essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but traditional error correction protocols are vulnerable to hardware defects and impose rigid connectivity constraints.
method: The authors propose a reset-free LUCI framework that asymmetrically scales the X or Z distance and uses two subroutine rounds for full syndrome extraction, then benchmark it on IBM quantum hardware against the standard rotated surface code.
result: The LUCI framework achieves error suppression of 0.79 for logical X errors and 0.82 for logical Z errors, compared to 0.73 and 0.76 for the standard approach, demonstrating competitive performance despite nearly halved syndrome density.
conclusion: Dynamic codes like LUCI can outperform standard methods by avoiding noisy components, challenging the dependency on static fault-tolerant architectures and paving the way for hybrid, hardware-compatible code designs.

title: Decoupling Band Topology From Criticality In Bosonic Systems
authors: Mariam Ughrelidze, Lorenza Viola, Emilio Cobanera
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A new understanding of criticality in systems described by quadratic bosonic Hamiltonians (QBHs) ties the emergence of long-range correlations to boundaries of dynamical, not thermodynamical, stability in the parameter space. This separation occurs because the solution of the Heisenberg equations of motion is determined by an auxiliary pseudo- Hermitian dynamical system. The boundary points of a region of dynamical stability can be either exceptional points, generically associated with long-range correlations, or Krein collisions, where correlations can be either long- or short-range. We investigate the interplay of this landscape of possibilities with band topology and boundary physics, by relying on both specific examples and general arguments. The examples stem from a two-parameter, thermodynamically unstable family of QBHs obtained from the bosonic Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model by breaking particle conservation while preserving a chiral pseudo-symmetry. The dynamically stable regime breaks up into different regions labeled by an integer-valued symplectic analogue of the Berry phase. The topological phase transition is a line of Krein collisions, which coincides with the closing of a band gap at zero and causes the localization length of the topologically mandated boundary zero modes to diverge before disappearing. In the unstable regime, we show that the chiral pseudo-symmetry of our model induces, despite the broken particle-number symmetry, enough structure on its associated dynamical matrices to support a topological classification and a bulk-boundary correspondence, independently of dynamical stability. This strongly suggests that bosonic topological physics extracted from basic index theory is insensitive to dynamical stability and, a posteriori, to non-interacting criticality.
tldr: This paper studies band topology and criticality in bosonic systems, focusing on dynamical stability and exceptional points, with no direct connection to quantum information theory.
motivation: The authors aim to decouple band topology from criticality in quadratic bosonic Hamiltonians, exploring the interplay of dynamical stability, exceptional points, and topological phases.
method: They analyze a two-parameter family of bosonic Su-Schrieffer-Heeger models with broken particle conservation, using symplectic Berry phases and pseudo-Hermitian dynamics.
result: They show that topological phase transitions coincide with Krein collisions, and that topological classification persists even in dynamically unstable regimes.
conclusion: Bosonic topological physics is insensitive to dynamical stability and non-interacting criticality, suggesting a separation between topology and critical phenomena.

title: Parent Hamiltonians Of Ergodic Matrix Product States
authors: Owen Ekblad, Eloy Moreno-Nadales, Eric B. Roon, Jeffrey H. Schenker
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matrix product states (MPS) are quintessential examples of frustration-free gapped ground states of local interactions called parent Hamiltonians. In this work, we investigate parent Hamiltonians for a class of ergodic matrix product states (EMPS), which are MPS defined by site-dependent random tensors [MATH] which are homogeneously distributed at every site [MATH] in the spin chain. Here, the EMPS are not translation-invariant but rather statistically translation-invariant. Under a mild injectivity assumption, we show the thermodynamic limit of an EMPS is the unique frustration-free ground state of a parent Hamiltonian on the whole spin chain, which, depending on the statistical properties of the EMPS, may or may not be finite-range. In contrast to the translation-invariant regime, these Hamiltonians need not be gapped. Nevertheless, applying the martingale method while keeping track of local statistics gives conditions for a gap, in addition to pointing towards why there need not be a gap in general. We include examples of EMPS both with and without spectral gaps to illustrate our results.
tldr: This paper studies parent Hamiltonians for ergodic matrix product states, focusing on their spectral gap properties.
motivation: To understand the ground state properties and spectral gaps of random, non-translation-invariant matrix product states.
method: Uses martingale methods and injectivity assumptions to analyze the thermodynamic limit and gap conditions for ergodic MPS.
result: Shows that ergodic MPS are unique frustration-free ground states of parent Hamiltonians, which may be finite-range or not, and may or may not have a spectral gap.
