conclusion: The spectral gap depends on statistical properties of the random tensors; examples with and without gaps are provided.

title: Generalized Rank Weight And Extended Generalized Poset Weight Defined For Codes Over Rings: A Galois Connection Approach
authors: Yang Xu, Haibin Kan, Guangyue Han
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study generalized rank weights (GRWs) and extended generalized poset weight (EGPWs) of codes over rings via a Galois connection approach. First, we show that various coding-theoretic properties related to generalized weights, including security drops of a code employed in wire-tap channel of type II, connections between generalized weights of a Gabidulin code and its associated Delsarte code, (generalized) Singleton bound, MDS discrepancy of a code, characterizations of MDS, near MDS, [MATH]-MDS, MRD, near MRD, [MATH]-MRD, (dually) quasi-MRD codes as well as evasive property of subspaces, can be reformulated in terms of Galois connections. Next, we study GRWs and rank profiles defined for modules over principal ideal rings, especially those over chain rings. Generalizing GRWs defined for vector spaces over fields, we establish a singleton bound and a Wei-type duality theorem, characterize MRD, near MRD and dually quasi-MRD codes and determine their GRWs; moreover, we characterize [MATH]-MRD codes and establish a scattered bound for [MATH]-evasive codes over chain rings, generalizing counterpart result established for vector space over finite fields. Finally, we propose and study EGPWs and extended poset profiles defined for modules with a composition series, which in fact form a Galois connection. Generalizing EGPWs defined for modules over finite Galois rings, we establish a Wei-type duality theorem for modules over arbitrary quasi-Frobenius rings, which unifies the two Wei-type duality theorems derived in both and .
tldr: This paper studies generalized rank weights and extended generalized poset weights for codes over rings using a Galois connection approach, focusing on coding-theoretic properties and wire-tap channel security.
motivation: To unify and generalize various coding-theoretic concepts related to generalized weights, including security drops and MDS/MRD codes, using a Galois connection framework.
method: The authors reformulate properties of generalized weights in terms of Galois connections, then extend the study to modules over principal ideal rings and quasi-Frobenius rings, establishing Singleton bounds and Wei-type duality theorems.
result: They derive Singleton bounds, Wei-type duality theorems, and characterizations of MRD, near MRD, and quasi-MRD codes over chain rings, as well as a scattered bound for evasive codes.
conclusion: The Galois connection approach provides a unified perspective on generalized weights, with results that generalize known theorems to more general algebraic structures.

title: Exact Quantum Time Compatible With Positive Energy
authors: Ovidiu Cristinel Stoica
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01296v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What would it be like to be in a superposition of yesterday, today, and tomorrow? This question may seem at best entertaining, but it is necessary, and exploring it allows us to understand how exact irreversible clocks and change are possible, despite the Unruh-Wald and Hegerfeldt-Ruijsenaars no-go theorems forbidding them. Unruh and Wald (1989) proved that if energy is bounded from below, no observable can increase monotonically with the Schr\"odinger time parameter t. Perfectly monotonic clocks and irreversible observable changes (Hegerfeldt-Ruijsenaars, 1980) seem impossible. From the perspective of the Schr\"odinger time, the world appears in a superposition of different intrinsic clock states indicating different times and opposite time directions. This seems to directly contradict our daily experiences of time and change. I show that there is no contradiction: from an intrinsic perspective of the world, sharp irreversible changes do happen, because the macroscopic pointer states resolve the superposition of different times. Large-scale time-reversing or discontinuous transitions are not internally observable in the records. From the intrinsic perspective, an unbounded intrinsic-time translation generator plays the role of the Hamiltonian, generating only forward time evolution with respect to the intrinsic time, but not to the Schr\"odinger parameter t, which is thus not justified to play the role of time. This allows sharp time observables even if the external Hamiltonian is bounded from below. In addition, this leads to a stationary wavefunction of the universe satisfying a Wheeler-DeWitt-type equation, without assuming gravity.
tldr: The paper proposes a resolution to no-go theorems against exact time observables by introducing an intrinsic time perspective, leading to a stationary Wheeler-DeWitt-type wavefunction.
motivation: No-go theorems by Unruh-Wald and Hegerfeldt-Ruijsenaars suggest that exact irreversible clocks and monotonic time observables are impossible if energy is bounded below, contradicting everyday experience of time and change.
method: The author distinguishes between external Schrödinger time and an intrinsic time generated by an unbounded operator, showing that macroscopic pointer states resolve superpositions of different intrinsic times, allowing sharp time observables.
result: Exact quantum time compatible with positive energy is possible from an intrinsic perspective, and the wavefunction of the universe becomes stationary, satisfying a Wheeler-DeWitt-type equation without assuming gravity.
conclusion: The apparent contradiction between no-go theorems and our experience of time is resolved by adopting an intrinsic time perspective, where irreversible changes occur internally even if the external Hamiltonian is bounded below.

title: A Fuzzy Sphere Journey In Critical Phenomena
authors: W. Zhu Yin-Chen He
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This review discusses the recently proposed fuzzy sphere regularization for studying [MATH]D critical phenomena, particularly three-dimensional (3D) conformal field theory (CFT). The fuzzy sphere scheme not only offers remarkable efficiency in extracting extensive CFT data at low computational cost but also reveals unexpected connections among 3D CFT (critical phenomena), noncommutative geometry, and the quantum Hall effect. We introduce the fundamental ideas of fuzzy sphere regularization, emphasizing its role in demonstrating the state-operator correspondence of 3D CFTs on the [MATH] geometry. Additionally, we review key developments in this approach across various directions and outline potential future applications.
tldr: A review of the fuzzy sphere regularization method for studying 3D critical phenomena and conformal field theory.
motivation: To introduce a novel numerical approach that efficiently extracts CFT data and reveals connections between 3D CFT, noncommutative geometry, and the quantum Hall effect.
method: The fuzzy sphere regularization maps the 3D CFT problem onto a 2D quantum Hall system on a sphere, leveraging noncommutative geometry to simulate the third dimension.
result: The method demonstrates state-operator correspondence for 3D CFTs and provides accurate CFT data at low computational cost.
conclusion: The fuzzy sphere approach is a powerful tool for studying 3D critical phenomena and may have broad applications in condensed matter and high-energy physics.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability And Causal Feature Steering Of Neural Quantum States Via Sparse Autoencoders
authors: Christopher Earls Zihao Qi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural Quantum States (NQS) are a remarkably expressive class of variational ans\"atze for quantum many-body wavefunctions, yet little is understood about their internal mechanisms: trained on variational objectives alone, how do NQS accurately capture physical observables that they have never been explicitly optimized for? In this work, we present a systematic approach to analyze the internal activations of NQS using sparse autoencoders. We extract features from the residual stream and demonstrate that these features strongly correlate with physical observables such as order parameters, staggered magnetization, and half-chain correlators, across both ground state representation and real-time dynamics. Remarkably, the discovery of these features is entirely unsupervised, with no physical labels provided. We further establish that such features causally affect the corresponding observables predicted by NQS, by showing that targeted, post-training intervention on a feature smoothly and monotonically steers the corresponding observable, while leaving the variational energy nearly unchanged. These results demonstrate that NQS are not merely functional approximators, but encode rich, interpretable internal representations of physical information. Our approach provides both a diagnostic and an intervention tool for NQS, and serves as a foundation for using mechanistic interpretability towards more reliable, transparent NQS.
tldr: This paper uses sparse autoencoders to interpret neural quantum states, finding that internal features correlate with physical observables.
motivation: Neural quantum states accurately predict observables they were not explicitly trained on, but their internal mechanisms are poorly understood.
method: Sparse autoencoders are applied to the residual stream of a neural quantum state to extract features, which are then correlated with physical observables and causally tested via feature steering.
result: Features correlate strongly with order parameters, staggered magnetization, and half-chain correlators; steering a feature smoothly changes the corresponding observable while preserving variational energy.
conclusion: Neural quantum states encode interpretable internal representations of physical information, enabling diagnostic and intervention tools for more reliable NQS.

title: Coherent States In Minimal-length Quantum Mechanics: Inequivalent Characterizations And Emergent Squeezing
authors: Giuseppe Gaetano Luciano, Pasquale Bosso, Daniel Chemisana
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several approaches to quantum gravity suggest the emergence of a fundamental minimal length at the Planck scale. In quantum mechanics, this feature is naturally encoded through deformations of the Heisenberg algebra, leading to the Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP). While the phenomenological implications of GUP have been extensively explored, a consistent characterization of coherent states in minimal-length quantum mechanics remains elusive. In this work, we present a systematic analysis of coherent states for the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator. We show that the canonical equivalence among their standard characterizations - as eigenstates of the annihilation operator, displaced vacuum states and minimum-uncertainty wave packets - is generically lost in the presence of a minimal length. We then investigate the dynamical and semiclassical consequences of this inequivalence by comparing the evolution of generalized coherent states with that of states saturating the GUP. In particular, we demonstrate that minimal-length effects induce nontrivial deformations of phase-space trajectories and give rise to an intrinsic squeezing mechanism with no counterpart in ordinary quantum mechanics. These results establish a unified framework for coherence in GUP-based quantum theories and identify distinctive semiclassical signatures of minimal-length physics, opening a new avenue for probing quantum-gravitational effects.
tldr: This paper studies coherent states in minimal-length quantum mechanics, showing that standard characterizations become inequivalent and that squeezing emerges due to the generalized uncertainty principle.
motivation: To provide a consistent characterization of coherent states in quantum mechanics with a minimal length, which is relevant to quantum gravity phenomenology.
method: Systematic analysis of coherent states for the 1D harmonic oscillator under GUP, comparing eigenstates of annihilation operator, displaced vacuum, and minimum-uncertainty wave packets.
result: The canonical equivalence among standard characterizations is lost; minimal-length effects deform phase-space trajectories and induce intrinsic squeezing.
conclusion: The work establishes a unified framework for coherence in GUP-based theories and identifies semiclassical signatures of minimal-length physics.

title: Influence Of The Radial Index On The Stability Of Laguerre-Gaussian Vortex Beams In Turbulent Media
authors: Aleksandr S. Losev, Anastasia Fominova, Natalia I. Matveeva
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper explores the selective suppression of Laguerre-Gaussian modes that are most vulnerable to atmospheric turbulence. Decomposing these modes into an orthogonal Zernike polynomial basis reveals significant differences in stability depending on the radial and azimuthal indices. We demonstrate that modes with a higher radial index exhibit minimal distortion of the transverse beam profile, providing a clear criterion for filtering out less resilient modes in turbulent media. Furthermore, we derive an analytical expression relating the required receiver aperture to the radial and azimuthal indices.
tldr: This paper studies the stability of Laguerre-Gaussian vortex beams in turbulent media, focusing on the effect of radial index.
motivation: Atmospheric turbulence distorts optical vortex beams, which are used in free-space optical communication. Understanding which modes are more resilient can improve communication link performance.
method: The authors decompose Laguerre-Gaussian modes into Zernike polynomials to analyze distortion, and derive an analytical expression for required receiver aperture size based on radial and azimuthal indices.
result: Modes with higher radial index exhibit less transverse profile distortion, providing a criterion for filtering out less resilient modes.
conclusion: The radial index is a key parameter for selecting robust modes in turbulent media, which can enhance free-space optical communication systems.

title: High-Beam-Quality Meta-Grating Couplers For Large Collimated Free-Space Beams On Silicon-on-Insulator
authors: Max Schittenhelm, Sebastian H\"afner, Steffen Sauer, Stefanie Kroker
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic integrated circuits on the silicon-on-insulator (SOI) platform typically interface with free space via grating couplers, but scaling these to collimated beams with diameters beyond 100 [MATH]m requires a fundamentally different regime of extremely weak, spatially distributed coupling. While such large-area couplers have been demonstrated, their beam quality has remained largely uncharacterized, even though applications such as coupling into high-finesse resonators or trapping of cold atoms require both a large aperture and a near-Gaussian profile. This article presents an SOI meta-grating coupler that emits collimated, near-Gaussian beams of approximately 300 [MATH]m waist diameter. The design synthesizes the required emission profile from a spatially tailored coupling strength, realized by locally varying a sub-wavelength unit cell while independently setting the local emission angle. This approach achieves the very low coupling strengths required for large beams and yields a measured beam quality of [MATH]. The scheme extends directly to other target profiles, such as flat-top or higher-order modes, rendering meta-grating couplers a practical chip-to-free-space interface for mode-matching-sensitive applications.
tldr: This paper presents a meta-grating coupler design on SOI for large collimated free-space beams with high beam quality.
motivation: Large-area grating couplers for photonic integrated circuits often have poor beam quality, limiting applications like coupling to high-finesse resonators or cold atom trapping.
method: The authors design a meta-grating with sub-wavelength unit cells that locally vary coupling strength and emission angle to synthesize a near-Gaussian profile.
result: They demonstrate a coupler emitting a collimated beam of ~300 μm waist diameter with measured beam quality M² close to 1.
conclusion: The meta-grating approach enables high-quality free-space beam emission from SOI chips, extendable to other beam profiles.

title: Learning Effective Soliton Dynamics From Scattering Data
authors: Seth Minor, Vanja Dukic, David M. Bortz
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The inverse scattering transform (IST) provides the standard theoretical framework for deriving soliton dynamics. Traditionally, such derivations have been of an analytical, rather than data-driven, nature. In this paper, we combine the conceptual framework of the IST with weak-form system identification methods to discover effective soliton dynamics directly from observed scattering data, without assuming prior knowledge of the scattering equations. Our method avoids parameterizing solitary waves via ad hoc curve-fitting by working in the scattering domain, yielding interpretable low-dimensional models that remain valid in perturbed and near-integrable regimes. We demonstrate the performance of the proposed approach on synthetic and experimental data governed by shallow-water equations of Korteweg--de Vries-type and recover models that are consistent with canonical IST theory.
tldr: This paper uses inverse scattering transform and system identification to learn soliton dynamics from data, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To derive effective soliton dynamics directly from observed scattering data without prior knowledge of scattering equations.
method: Combines inverse scattering transform framework with weak-form system identification methods to discover low-dimensional models from data.
result: Demonstrates recovery of models consistent with canonical IST theory on synthetic and experimental shallow-water wave data.
conclusion: The approach yields interpretable models valid in perturbed regimes, but is purely classical and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Identical-Particle Symmetry-Enabled Complete Coherent Control Of Ultracold Atomic And Molecular Collisions
authors: Jing-Chen Zhang, Adrien Devolder, Timur V. Tscherbul, Paul Brumer, Yu Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that exchange symmetry in collisions of identical particles enables symmetry-protected coherent control of the total scattering cross section. For identical fermions, antisymmetrization enforces complete phase synchronization of the contributing scattering channels, yielding maximal control visibility. For identical bosons, synchronization persists but with reduced visibility due to additional exchange (satellite) contributions. Collisions of distinguishable particles lack this symmetry-imposed phase locking, leading to lower controllability and visibility. We elucidate these principles through coupled-channel quantum-scattering calculations for lithium-lithium collisions, comparing the [MATH]-[MATH] (identical fermions), [MATH]-[MATH] (identical bosons), and [MATH]-[MATH] (distinguishable) systems. Furthermore, in the identical particle cases, symmetry-enforced synchronization enables full control over the parity of the final state at any collisional energy. This mechanism is broadly applicable to identical-particle collisions, including homonuclear molecules for which established approaches -- DC electric fields, or microwave shielding -- are ineffective or unavailable.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that exchange symmetry in collisions of identical particles enables complete coherent control of scattering cross sections, with applications to ultracold atomic and molecular collisions.
motivation: To achieve coherent control over ultracold collisions, especially for homonuclear molecules where established methods like DC fields or microwave shielding are ineffective.
method: The authors use coupled-channel quantum-scattering calculations for lithium-lithium collisions, comparing identical fermions, identical bosons, and distinguishable particles to illustrate the role of exchange symmetry.
result: Exchange symmetry enforces phase synchronization of scattering channels, leading to maximal control visibility for fermions and reduced but significant visibility for bosons, while distinguishable particles lack this effect.
conclusion: Symmetry-enforced synchronization enables full control over the parity of the final state at any collisional energy, providing a broadly applicable mechanism for controlling identical-particle collisions.

title: Hypergraph Minority Game With Local Hyperedge Payoffs
authors: Fanyuan Meng Yihang Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide a theoretical derivation of the Hypergraph Minority Game with Local Hyperedge Payoffs (HMG-L), in which [MATH] adaptive agents compete simultaneously in multiple overlapping groups modeled as hyperedges of a static hypergraph [MATH]. Each hyperedge constitutes an independent local minority game, and agents accumulate payoffs across all groups to which they belong. We derive the continuum-time limit of the score dynamics, from which we obtain a set of coupled nonlinear stochastic differential equations for the agents' strategy polarization variables. The deterministic drift is shown to derive from a global cost function that generalizes the standard Minority Game Hamiltonian to hypergraph-structured interactions. We perform a sparse-annealed replica analysis of the stationary state for the case of a [MATH]-uniform, [MATH]-regular random hypergraph, obtaining the saddle-point equations within the replica-symmetric ansatz, an explicit replicon stability criterion, and Bethe/cavity equations for sparse corrections. The leading sparse-regime transition occurs on a critical surface [MATH], while the globally coupled MG value [MATH] is recovered only in the separate single-hyperedge limit. We derive expressions for the order parameters -- global volatility [MATH], predictability [MATH], hyperedge frustration [MATH], and frozen fraction [MATH] -- and discuss their scaling behavior near criticality. The Fokker-Planck equation governing finite-[MATH] fluctuations is presented, and the noise covariance matrix is computed from the hypergraph structure. Limiting cases ([MATH], [MATH], [MATH]) are analyzed in detail, establishing connections to the standard MG, networked MG, and parallel MG models.
tldr: This paper extends the Minority Game to hypergraph-structured interactions with local hyperedge payoffs, analyzing collective behavior via statistical physics methods.
motivation: The Minority Game models adaptive agents competing in a market; this work generalizes it to multiple overlapping groups to capture more complex social or economic interactions.
method: The authors derive continuum-limit score dynamics, perform replica analysis for a uniform random hypergraph, and obtain saddle-point equations, replicon stability, and Bethe/cavity equations.
result: They find a critical surface for the phase transition, compute order parameters like volatility and predictability, and recover standard MG limits.
conclusion: The hypergraph extension reveals new scaling behavior and connects to networked and parallel MG models, but remains within the realm of agent-based modeling and statistical physics of complex systems.

title: Beyond Degree: Rooted Motif Signatures For Latent Position Identifiability In Graphon Models
authors: Tabea Rebafka Roland Boniface Sogan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graphon estimation requires structural assumptions to address its intrinsic non-identifiability. A standard approach is degree-based identifiability, where the degree function is assumed to be strictly monotonic. This assumption is rather restrictive and fails for graphons with constant or non-injective degree function, even when distinct latent positions have different connectivity profiles. In this paper, we introduce as higher-order node-level representations for graphons. They extend the degree function by recording, at each latent position, the densities of rooted motifs such as triangles, cycles, paths, and other local subgraph patterns. We study the extent to which these signatures can distinguish latent positions beyond degree information. For generic finite-rank graphons, we prove that suitable rooted motif signatures determine the connectivity profiles of latent positions. We also explain why such a property cannot hold for arbitrary graphons without additional assumptions, since different latent positions may have identical rooted motif signatures. On the statistical side, we define empirical rooted motif signatures from a single observed graph and prove uniform concentration bounds for these estimators. Simulation experiments illustrate that rooted motif signatures can reveal latent structure in settings where degree-based representations are uninformative, including graphons with constant or non-injective degree functions and stochastic block models with equal block degrees.
tldr: This paper introduces rooted motif signatures for latent position identifiability in graphon models, a topic in network analysis and graph theory.
motivation: Degree-based identifiability in graphon estimation is restrictive; the authors aim to provide higher-order node-level representations to distinguish latent positions with identical degree functions.
method: They define rooted motif signatures recording densities of local subgraph patterns (triangles, cycles, paths) and prove that for generic finite-rank graphons these signatures determine connectivity profiles, with concentration bounds for empirical estimators.
result: Rooted motif signatures can reveal latent structure in settings where degree-based representations fail, such as graphons with constant degree or stochastic block models with equal block degrees.
conclusion: Rooted motif signatures offer a more expressive tool for graphon identifiability, though they cannot distinguish all graphons without additional assumptions.

title: Linking Effective Ratner Equidistribution To The Semicircle Law For Skew-shift Matrices
authors: Yong Li Cong Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider large Hermitian matrices whose entries are defined by evaluating the exponential function along orbits of the skew-shift \({2}\omega + jy + x \mod 1\) for irrational \(\omega\). We establish a rigorous connection between the effective Ratner equidistribution theorem for unipotent orbits in \(\SL(3,\R)/\SL(3,\Z)\) and the global semicircle law for such deterministic matrices. For frequency sequences satisfying a Diophantine condition, we prove that the empirical spectral distribution of these matrices converges to the Wigner semicircle law with optimal polynomial rate \(O(N^{-1})\); for rectangular matrices the corresponding Marchenko--Pastur law is obtained. The proof uses a multi-parameter effective mixing property derived from the effective Ratner equidistribution theorem, combined with a graph-theoretic expansion of the moments. Our results evidence the quasirandom nature of the skew-shift dynamics observed in other contexts by Bourgain, Goldstein and Schlag, and Rudnick, Sarnak and Zaharescu, and provide a dynamical systems proof of the semicircle law with an improved convergence rate.
tldr: This paper proves the semicircle law for deterministic matrices from skew-shift dynamics using effective Ratner equidistribution.
motivation: To understand spectral properties of deterministic matrices arising from dynamical systems and to provide a dynamical proof of the semicircle law with optimal convergence rate.
method: Combines effective Ratner equidistribution for unipotent orbits in SL(3,R)/SL(3,Z) with a graph-theoretic moment expansion.
result: Empirical spectral distribution converges to Wigner semicircle law with rate O(N^{-1}) for Hermitian matrices; Marchenko-Pastur law for rectangular matrices.
conclusion: The skew-shift dynamics exhibit quasirandom behavior, and the semicircle law can be derived from dynamical systems theory with improved convergence.

title: Generative Ai And Federated Learning For Intrusion Detection Systems: A Survey
authors: Jiefei Liu, Abu Saleh Md Tayeen, Pratyay Kumar, Qixu Gong, Wenbin Jiang, Huiping Cao, Satyajayant Misra, Jayashree Harikumar
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) are essential for monitoring network traffic and identifying malicious activities in modern cyber-physical, Internet of Things (IoT), enterprise, and distributed network environments. However, developing reliable IDS models remains challenging because attack behaviors evolve over time, realistic datasets are difficult to obtain, traffic records may be incomplete, attack classes are often imbalanced, and privacy constraints limit centralized data collection. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) and Federated Learning (FL) provide new opportunities to address these limitations. Generative models can support anomaly detection, synthetic traffic generation, data augmentation, data imputation, adversarial traffic generation, and IDS alert explanation. FL enables distributed IDS training without directly sharing local network traffic, making it suitable for privacy-sensitive and geographically distributed environments. This survey provides a structured review of generative AI and FL techniques for IDS. We first summarize representative IDS research directions, including adversarial machine learning, anomaly-based detection, IoT-oriented IDS, explainable IDS, and benchmark datasets. We then categorize generative AI applications in IDS according to model families and task objectives, covering autoencoder-based models, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), diffusion models, and Large Language Models (LLMs). Finally, we review emerging studies that integrate generative AI with FL-based IDS and discuss open challenges, including synthetic data quality, realistic traffic generation, dual-use adversarial risks, non-IID client distributions, communication-efficient model sharing, federated IDS benchmarking, and domain-specific LLMs for network security.
tldr: A survey on using generative AI and federated learning for intrusion detection systems.
motivation: Intrusion detection systems face challenges like evolving attacks, scarce data, and privacy constraints; generative AI and FL offer potential solutions.
method: The paper categorizes generative AI applications (autoencoders, GANs, diffusion models, LLMs) and FL-based IDS, reviewing existing literature.
result: Identifies key applications and open challenges such as synthetic data quality, non-IID distributions, and communication efficiency.
conclusion: Generative AI and FL can enhance IDS, but significant challenges remain in data quality, adversarial risks, and benchmarking.

title: Self-Referential $k$-sat And The Finite Analogue Of G\"odel's Incompleteness Theorem
authors: Wen Fang, Xianxian Li, Jun Liu, Jie Luo, Yongxin Tong, Ke Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-reference and solution independence are core properties underlying intractability. This paper establishes a finite combinatorial analogue of G\"odel's incompleteness theorems within Boolean [MATH]-SAT. While standard random [MATH]-SAT has assignment correlations that disrupt solution independence, we resolve this via a logarithmic-width ensemble ([MATH]). Here, satisfying assignments converge to a Poisson distribution, letting unsatisfiable and uniquely satisfiable formulas coexist. By executing a single-clause substitution conditioned on the unique solution, we construct structurally irreducible SAT/UNSAT pairs that are indistinguishable via local evaluation. Using algorithmic information theory and Shannon channels, we prove that deductive pipelines restricted to a sublinear window suffer from an informational blind spot, forcing a descriptive lower bound of [MATH]. This deficit forces any Resolution refutation of the UNSAT instance to utilize wide clauses ([MATH]), triggering an exponential proof-tree explosion ([MATH]). As [MATH], this bound converges to the worst-case [MATH] threshold, reframing the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) as a direct projection of G\"odel incompleteness onto finite computation. We diagnose the decades-long stagnation in complexity theory. Transitioning from Turing's class separation to a G\"odelian paradigm of instance indistinguishability, we introduce a multi-dimensional comparative framework that contrasts these two historical lineages across distinct perspectives. The self-referential hardness exhibits physical invariance: it precludes quantum shortcuts due to the necessity of global semantic analysis and delineates a scaling bottleneck for machine learning architectures operating on lossy, local compression.
tldr: This paper establishes a finite combinatorial analogue of Gödel's incompleteness theorems within Boolean k-SAT, linking self-referential hardness to computational complexity.
motivation: To understand the fundamental source of intractability in SAT and complexity theory, and to reframe SETH as a projection of Gödel incompleteness.
method: Constructs structurally irreducible SAT/UNSAT pairs via a logarithmic-width ensemble and single-clause substitution, then uses algorithmic information theory and Shannon channels to prove an informational blind spot for local deduction.
result: Any Resolution refutation of the UNSAT instance requires wide clauses, leading to exponential proof-tree explosion, and the bound converges to the worst-case threshold as n grows.
conclusion: The self-referential hardness precludes quantum shortcuts and delineates a scaling bottleneck for machine learning, suggesting a paradigm shift from Turing-style class separation to Gödelian instance indistinguishability.

title: Unveiling The Non-Monotonic Effect Of Privacy On Generalization Under Byzantine Robustness
authors: Thomas Boudou, Batiste Le Bars, Nirupam Gupta, Aur\'elien Bellet
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01492v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent work has established a fundamental trilemma between Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy (LDP), and optimization error in distributed learning. We show that this trilemma does not universally extend to generalization error, but instead depends critically on the privacy regime. Specifically, in the high-noise regime (strong privacy), we prove that increasing privacy reduces the generalization error, i.e., there is no tension between robustness and privacy. In the low-noise regime (weaker privacy), however, the tension between robustness and privacy reappears and increasing privacy indeed degrades generalization. Our theory explains this surprising non-monotonic behavior of the generalization error via matching lower and upper bounds on the algorithmic stability of Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints. We corroborate and further analyze these theoretical findings with empirical evaluations.
tldr: This paper studies the non-monotonic effect of privacy on generalization in Byzantine-robust distributed learning, showing that the trilemma between robustness, privacy, and optimization error does not universally extend to generalization.
motivation: Recent work established a trilemma between Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy, and optimization error in distributed learning. This paper investigates whether this trilemma extends to generalization error.
method: The authors derive matching lower and upper bounds on the algorithmic stability of Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints, analyzing the generalization error in high-noise and low-noise privacy regimes.
result: In the high-noise (strong privacy) regime, increasing privacy reduces generalization error, showing no tension. In the low-noise (weaker privacy) regime, increasing privacy degrades generalization, revealing a tension.
conclusion: The trilemma between robustness, privacy, and generalization is not universal; it depends critically on the privacy regime, with non-monotonic behavior explained by stability bounds.

title: Towards Learning Representations Of Policies In Two-Player Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games
authors: Kevin Wang, Kevin Yang, Arjun Prakash, Amy Greenwald
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01498v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the problem of learning useful policy representations (embeddings) in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games. We make three contributions: First, we introduce methods of creating datasets of policies for a given game. Second, we propose methods to learn policy representations. Third, we introduce downstream tasks to evaluate the effectiveness of such representations. We evaluate each dataset method, embedding method, and downstream task on Kuhn and Leduc Poker. Although our methods are very basic, we demonstrate that useful behavioral representations are present in the learned embeddings. To our knowledge, this work is among the first to systematically compare self-supervised learning techniques for learning policy representations in games. Our code is available at [URL] for others to extend.
tldr: This paper explores learning policy representations in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games using self-supervised learning.
motivation: The authors aim to systematically compare self-supervised learning techniques for learning behavioral representations of policies in game theory settings.
method: They create datasets of policies for Kuhn and Leduc Poker, propose embedding methods, and evaluate on downstream tasks.
result: Basic methods demonstrate that useful behavioral representations are present in the learned embeddings.
conclusion: This work is among the first to systematically compare self-supervised learning for policy representations in games, providing a foundation for future research.

title: Testing Unate Distributions
authors: Daeho Lee, Shivam Nadimpalli, Mingda Qiao, Ronitt Rubinfeld
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01573v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We initiate the study of *unate distributions* over [MATH] -- a natural analogue of unate Boolean functions -- by considering two basic testing problems that parallel well-studied questions for monotone distributions: - Uniformity Testing of Unate Distributions: We show that [MATH] samples are sufficient and necessary, in contrast to the [MATH] sample complexity of the analogous problem for monotone distributions (Rubinfeld and Servedio, STOC 2005; Adamaszek, Czumaj, and Sohler, SODA 2010). - Unateness Testing of Arbitrary Distributions: We give a tester that uses [MATH] conditional samples in the subcube conditional model. On the other hand, every tester that draws conditional samples in a similar fashion, namely from [MATH]-dimensional subcubes, must have an [MATH] complexity. In the same model, the complexity of monotonicity testing was recently shown to be [MATH] (Chakrabarty et al., STOC 2025). Our algorithms for both problems significantly outperform the naive approach of reducing to the monotone case, which would incur [MATH] sample complexity. Our uniformity tester relies on a subroutine that "weakly" learns the hidden orientations of a unate distribution, together with a new correlation bound for these estimates. Both tools may be of independent interest in studying monotonicity and unateness over [MATH].
tldr: This paper initiates the study of unate distributions over the hypercube and provides sample complexity bounds for uniformity and unateness testing.
motivation: Unate distributions are a natural generalization of monotone distributions, and understanding their testability is a fundamental question in distribution testing.
method: The paper develops a uniformity tester that uses a subroutine to weakly learn hidden orientations of a unate distribution, combined with a new correlation bound. For unateness testing, it uses conditional samples from subcubes.
result: The uniformity tester uses O(n) samples, which is optimal, contrasting with the exponential sample complexity for monotone distributions. The unateness tester uses O(n) conditional samples, and a lower bound shows that any tester using subcube conditional samples must have exponential complexity.
conclusion: Unate distributions are significantly easier to test than monotone distributions in the standard sampling model, but remain hard in the conditional sampling model.

title: Interferometric Characterization Of The Relative Phase Between Two X-ray Free-electron Laser Pulses Using Long-lived M\"ossbauer Resonances
authors: J\"org Evers Lukas Wolff
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coherence-based spectroscopy methods are powerful tools to explore structure and dynamics of matter. However, towards higher photon energies, the generation of sequences of pulses with well-characterized relative delays and phases remains a challenge. Here, we introduce a method to measure the relative phase [MATH] between subsequent transform-limited pulses from high-repetition-rate x-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs). It is based on a Ramsey-type interference measurement, enabled by introducing long-lived M\"ossbauer resonances into the XFEL beam path up- or downstream a primary experiment, which allow one to bridge the temporal gap between the XFEL pulses. The measured phase can be used as additional input for the analysis of the primary experiment.
tldr: This paper introduces a method to measure the relative phase between two X-ray free-electron laser pulses using long-lived Mössbauer resonances.
motivation: Coherence-based spectroscopy at high photon energies requires well-characterized pulse sequences, but generating such sequences with known relative delays and phases is challenging.
method: A Ramsey-type interference measurement is performed by placing long-lived Mössbauer resonances in the XFEL beam path to bridge the temporal gap between pulses.
result: The method enables characterization of the relative phase between subsequent transform-limited XFEL pulses.
conclusion: The measured phase can be used as additional input for analyzing primary experiments, enhancing coherence-based spectroscopy at XFELs.

title: Fourier-Diagonalized Natural Gradients And Sobolev Mirror Descent
authors: Jeongbin Jo
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study natural-gradient updates whose metric operators are diagonalized by the Fourier transform and relate them to Sobolev mirror descent. Translation-invariant Fisher geometries and Sobolev mirror geometries share a common inverse-map structure in the spectral domain. The Fisher metric is represented by a positive Fourier symbol, while Sobolev mirror geometry corresponds to the specific Bessel-potential symbol associated with the Sobolev norm. When these symbols coincide, the natural-gradient and mirror-descent updates are identical; otherwise, Sobolev mirror descent provides a canonical spectral preconditioner for the Fisher inverse geometry. This gives a mathematical lens through which spectral filtering and truncation techniques in PDE and operator learning can be viewed as natural actions of inverse metric geometry. We introduce Spectral Natural Gradient, an FFT-based implementation of these geometric updates.
tldr: The paper studies natural-gradient updates with Fourier-diagonalized metrics and relates them to Sobolev mirror descent, focusing on optimization theory rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To unify natural-gradient and mirror-descent methods via spectral analysis and provide efficient FFT-based implementations.
method: The authors analyze translation-invariant Fisher geometries and Sobolev mirror geometries in the spectral domain, showing they share an inverse-map structure, and introduce Spectral Natural Gradient using FFT.
result: When Fisher and Sobolev symbols coincide, updates are identical; otherwise, Sobolev mirror descent acts as a spectral preconditioner. The method is applied to PDE and operator learning.
conclusion: The work provides a mathematical lens for spectral filtering in optimization but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Structure-Preserving Reduced-Order Modeling Via Low-Rank Transport Signatures
authors: Jiajia Yu, Jingwei Hu, Fengyan Li, Shanyin Tong, Yunan Yang, Zhaiming Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parametrized PDEs with density-valued solutions are often difficult to approximate with classical linear reduced-order models, especially in transport-dominated regimes. We introduce an optimal-transport-based reduced-order modeling that represents each density by the Kantorovich potential transporting a fixed reference density to the target density, and then maps these potentials to transport signatures using a weighted Laplacian associated with the reference measure. This embeds the density-valued solution map in a Hilbert space while preserving control of the induced transport maps and Wasserstein error. We treat the signature map as a continuous matrix indexed by parameters and space, construct a low-rank skeleton decomposition using a maximal-volume criterion, and learn the parameter-to-coefficient map with a neural network for efficient non-intrusive online evaluation. The reconstructed solution is obtained by pushing forward the reference density, so mass preservation is built into the method. We prove a mean-squared Wasserstein error bound separating low-rank approximation, discretization, sampling, and learning errors, and demonstrate the method on a two-dimensional continuity equation, where transport signatures yield substantially lower-rank structure than the original density snapshots.
tldr: This paper proposes an optimal-transport-based reduced-order modeling method for parametrized PDEs with density-valued solutions, using Kantorovich potentials and low-rank skeleton decomposition.
motivation: Classical linear reduced-order models struggle with transport-dominated regimes and density-valued solutions; a structure-preserving method is needed.
method: Represent each density by the Kantorovich potential transporting a reference density to the target, map potentials to transport signatures via a weighted Laplacian, then construct a low-rank skeleton decomposition and learn the parameter-to-coefficient map with a neural network.
result: The method preserves mass, yields lower-rank structure than original snapshots, and a mean-squared Wasserstein error bound is proved.
conclusion: The approach effectively handles transport-dominated problems and provides a non-intrusive, efficient online evaluation.

title: Low-Latency Task-Oriented Image Transmission With Opportunistic Spectrum Access
authors: Jo\~ao Henrique Inacio de Souza, Mattia Merluzzi, Mateus P. Mota, Beatriz Soret, Petar Popovski
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Communication systems designed for reliable data reconstruction, rather than task-oriented communication, typically rely on separate source and channel coding and incur high latency under limited spectrum availability and fading channels. To address this, we propose a transmission framework with opportunistic spectrum access, in which the transmitter sends discrete latent representations learned via a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) over idle licensed channels using standard digital modulation. The AI-powered receiver is still able to reconstruct task-related information from the heavily compressed data. We develop a cross-layer latency model that accounts for compression, block errors, retransmissions, and stochastic channel access. Results on latency-accuracy trade-offs show that the proposed scheme achieves at least 79- and 3.3-fold latency reductions with only 5.7% and 2.4% drops in classification accuracy compared to benchmarks using conventional source and channel coding. The framework enables low-latency communication and reliable task execution even under limited spectrum availability and challenging channel conditions.
tldr: A task-oriented image transmission framework using VQ-VAE and opportunistic spectrum access to reduce latency.
motivation: Conventional communication systems designed for reliable data reconstruction incur high latency under limited spectrum and fading channels.
method: The transmitter sends discrete latent representations from a VQ-VAE over idle licensed channels using digital modulation; a cross-layer latency model accounts for compression, block errors, retransmissions, and stochastic channel access.
result: The scheme achieves 79-fold and 3.3-fold latency reductions with only 5.7% and 2.4% drops in classification accuracy compared to benchmarks.
conclusion: The framework enables low-latency communication and reliable task execution under limited spectrum availability and challenging channel conditions.

title: Partition Rank And Algebraic Circuit Lower Bounds
authors: Cornelius Brand, Petteri Kaski, Jiaheng Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strassen's theory of bilinear complexity provides a mathematical characterization of the arithmetic complexity of primitives such as matrix multiplication via the rank of tensors. However, the connection to tensor rank is known to break down in higher degrees of multilinearity. In this work, we highlight an unexplored connection between a generalized notion of tensor rank, which can be defined in Naslund's framework of partition ranks (JCTA 2020), and multiplicative complexity. These partition ranks allow us to control the multiplicative complexity, and thus arithmetic complexity, in any constant degree of multilinearity from below, while recovering Strassen's seminal characterization in the bilinear case. This enables novel potential applications of the rank-based approaches to problems in fine-grained algorithms and complexity, such as the hyperclique conjecture of Lincoln-Williams-Vassilevska Williams (SODA 2018). Moreover, we exhibit connections to established notions of rank, such as tensor slice rank (in the sense of Tao and Sawin), as well as its symmetric variant. For computing the latter symmetric variant, we point out a simple NP-hardness proof, contrasting the rather involved NP-hardness proof for ordinary, non-symmetric tensor slice rank by Bl\"aser et al. (SODA 2021).
tldr: This paper explores connections between partition ranks and algebraic circuit lower bounds, focusing on multiplicative complexity and tensor rank generalizations.
motivation: Strassen's bilinear complexity theory breaks down for higher multilinearity; the authors seek a generalized rank notion to control multiplicative complexity in constant-degree multilinearity.
method: They use Naslund's partition rank framework to define a generalized tensor rank and analyze its relation to multiplicative complexity, also connecting to slice rank and symmetric variants.
result: Partition ranks provide lower bounds on multiplicative complexity for any constant degree of multilinearity, recovering Strassen's bilinear case, and they show NP-hardness for computing symmetric slice rank.
conclusion: The work opens potential applications to fine-grained complexity problems like the hyperclique conjecture, but remains within algebraic complexity theory rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Mean Field Reinforcement Learning
authors: Mathieu Lauri\`ere Ren\'e Carmona
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This monograph provides an introduction to mean field reinforcement learning through the lens of Markov decision processes arising from large-population stochastic control with mean field interactions and common noise. Starting from the connection between multi-agent reinforcement learning and mean field control, it develops the probabilistic, mathematical, and control-theoretic framework needed to formulate representative-agent learning problems, analyze their relationship with finite-population systems, and study both general and linear-quadratic models. The presentation includes dynamic programming principles, propagation-of-chaos limits, and theoretical analyses of tabular Q-learning and policy-gradient methods. It also discusses numerical implementations, including tabular schemes and deep reinforcement learning methods such as deep deterministic policy gradient. The goal is to give readers a coherent bridge between mean field control theory and reinforcement learning methodology, emphasizing the mathematical structure of the problems and the design of tractable learning approaches for large stochastic populations.
tldr: This monograph introduces mean field reinforcement learning, bridging multi-agent RL and mean field control theory.
motivation: To provide a coherent mathematical framework for reinforcement learning in large-population stochastic control problems with mean field interactions.
method: Develops probabilistic and control-theoretic foundations, including dynamic programming, propagation of chaos, and analysis of tabular Q-learning and policy-gradient methods.
result: Presents theoretical analyses and numerical implementations for mean field RL, including linear-quadratic models and deep RL methods.
conclusion: The monograph offers a structured bridge between mean field control and RL, enabling tractable learning approaches for large stochastic populations.

title: Laser Stabilized To A Room Temperature Cavity With AlGaAs Coatings Reaching $4.2 \times 10^{-17}$ Fractional Frequency Instability
authors: Chun Yu Ma, Jialiang Yu, Steffen Sauer, Thomas Legero, Daniele Nicolodi, Mona Kempkes, Sofia Herbers, Fritz Riehle, Uwe Sterr
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a laser system referenced to a room-temperature ultrastable cavity employing crystalline AlGaAs coatings. We demonstrate a fractional frequency instability of [MATH], which is one of the lowest for room temperature systems and surpasses the limit imposed by Brownian noise if dielectric coatings were employed. For the first time in a room temperature system we identified the spontaneous fluctuations of the coating birefringence as a leading contribution to frequency instability. At optimized conditions we achieve an ultrastable cavity with an eigenfrequency that is highly immune to power fluctuations. As acceleration noise is the main noise contribution, we demonstrated that a feed-forward method can reduce the influence of accelerations on the cavity-stabilized laser frequency by a factor of four.
tldr: This paper presents a laser system stabilized to a room-temperature cavity with AlGaAs coatings, achieving ultra-low frequency instability.
motivation: To improve the stability of laser systems for precision metrology and timekeeping by reducing thermal noise and other instabilities.
method: The authors use a room-temperature ultrastable cavity with crystalline AlGaAs coatings and characterize its frequency instability, identifying coating birefringence fluctuations as a noise source.
result: They achieve a fractional frequency instability of 4.2e-17, surpassing the Brownian noise limit of dielectric coatings, and demonstrate a feed-forward method to reduce acceleration noise by a factor of four.
conclusion: The system offers one of the lowest instabilities for room-temperature cavities, with potential applications in optical clocks and precision measurements.

title: Small Denominators And Subresonant Accumulation In Weakly Nonlinear Dispersive Dynamics
authors: O. M. Kiselev P. Yu. Astafieva
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a small-denominator mechanism in weakly nonlinear dispersive dynamics. After Fourier decomposition, a nonlinear dispersive equation becomes an infinite system of weakly coupled oscillators. Higher-order correction terms may then contain infinite families of nonresonant Fourier interactions whose detunings tend to zero. Such families do not produce exact secular terms, but their accumulated contribution may grow as a power of time. We call this effect subresonant accumulation. The rigorous part of the paper is the analysis of a model forced oscillator and of an abstract subresonant Duhamel sum. If the detuning and coefficients have the form [MATH] and [MATH], then the accumulated contribution grows as [MATH], where [MATH]. We then show how this mechanism appears in a quartic Fourier family for the Klein--Gordon dispersion law. For the full nonlinear partial differential equation we formulate a conditional approximation result: provided that all remaining resonant and almost resonant interactions are controlled, the subresonant term gives the leading long-time correction.
tldr: This paper studies a small-denominator mechanism in weakly nonlinear dispersive dynamics, focusing on subresonant accumulation in Fourier interactions.
motivation: To understand how nonresonant Fourier interactions with detunings tending to zero can lead to growing contributions over time, potentially affecting long-time behavior of nonlinear dispersive equations.
method: The authors analyze a model forced oscillator and an abstract subresonant Duhamel sum, then demonstrate the mechanism in a quartic Fourier family for the Klein-Gordon dispersion law.
result: The accumulated contribution grows as t^α where α depends on the detuning and coefficients; a conditional approximation result is formulated for the full PDE.
conclusion: Subresonant accumulation can provide the leading long-time correction in weakly nonlinear dispersive dynamics, provided other resonant interactions are controlled.

title: Symbolic Discovery Of Iterative Algorithms: A Continuous Latent Space Bayesian Optimization Framework
authors: Ilias Mitrai Tongjia Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we consider the automated discovery of iterative optimization algorithms. We formulate the algorithm discovery task as a discrete optimization problem and search for new update functions using latent space Bayesian Optimization. The proposed framework first learns a continuous representation of the discrete space of update functions using variational autoencoders, transforming the algorithm discovery task from a discrete to a continuous search problem. The continuous representation is subsequently used to search for new algorithms using Bayesian optimization. Application to two case studies shows that the proposed approach can discover new update functions in symbolic form without any assumptions on the functional form of the update function. Moreover, the computational time required to discover the new update functions is lower than existing mathematical programming-based approaches.
tldr: This paper proposes a framework for automated discovery of iterative optimization algorithms using latent space Bayesian optimization.
motivation: Manually designing optimization algorithms is time-consuming and requires expertise; automating the discovery process can lead to novel and efficient algorithms.
method: The framework uses variational autoencoders to learn a continuous representation of the discrete space of update functions, then applies Bayesian optimization to search for new algorithms in this continuous space.
result: The approach discovers new update functions in symbolic form without prior assumptions, and with lower computational cost than existing mathematical programming-based methods.
conclusion: The proposed framework is effective for automated algorithm discovery and can be applied to various optimization problems.

title: On The Power Set Of Quasinilpotent Operators In Banach Spaces
authors: C. L. Hu, Y. Q. Ji, D. H. Liang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a quasinilpotent operator [MATH] on a Banach space [MATH], Douglas and Yang defined [MATH] for each non-zero vector [MATH], and called [MATH] the power set of [MATH]. In this paper, we prove that [MATH] always contains [MATH] for every quasinilpotent operator [MATH] on [MATH]. Moreover, we introduce the concept of a Banach space [MATH] having uniform multiplicity infinity and prove that some classical Banach spaces possess this property. As an application, we show that if [MATH] is right closed and contains [MATH], then there exists a quasinilpotent operator [MATH] on a class of Banach spaces with uniform multiplicity infinity such that [MATH].
tldr: This paper studies the power set of quasinilpotent operators on Banach spaces, a topic in functional analysis with no connection to quantum information theory.
motivation: To characterize the set of values of a quasinilpotent operator applied to a vector, and to introduce the concept of uniform multiplicity infinity in Banach spaces.
method: The authors prove that the power set always contains the origin, define Banach spaces with uniform multiplicity infinity, and show that certain classical Banach spaces have this property.
result: The power set of any quasinilpotent operator contains zero, and for right-closed sets containing zero, there exists a quasinilpotent operator on a Banach space with uniform multiplicity infinity whose power set equals that set.
conclusion: The paper contributes to operator theory and Banach space geometry, but is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: On The Structure Of Constacyclic Codes Over Finite Chain Rings
authors: Vaishali Singh, Sucheta Dutt, Ridhima Thakral
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01771v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the present paper, we provide an explicit construction for generators of a [MATH]-constacyclic code [MATH] of arbitrary length [MATH] over a finite chain ring(FCR) [MATH] in terms of certain minimum degree polynomials of the ring [MATH]. Moreover, the proposed construction achieves the minimum possible number of generators. We prove certain properties of this set of generators, using which we obtain a minimal spanning set of [MATH]. We also obtain that the rank of [MATH] is [MATH], where [MATH] is the degree of the minimal degree polynomial in [MATH]. Finally, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions under which an arbitrary length [MATH]-constacyclic code [MATH] over [MATH] is Maximum Hamming Distance with respect to Rank(MHDR) as well as Maximum Distance Separable(MDS) in terms of a torsion code of [MATH] over the residue field [MATH] of [MATH]. We further determine the exact values for [MATH] for which [MATH] over [MATH] is MHDR.
tldr: This paper studies the algebraic structure of constacyclic codes over finite chain rings, focusing on generator sets and distance properties.
motivation: To provide an explicit construction for generators of constacyclic codes over finite chain rings with minimal number of generators, and to characterize MHDR and MDS codes.
method: Uses algebraic methods to construct generators from minimum degree polynomials, derive a minimal spanning set, and relate code properties to torsion codes over the residue field.
result: Achieves minimal generator sets, expresses rank in terms of polynomial degree, and gives necessary and sufficient conditions for MHDR and MDS codes.
conclusion: The work contributes to coding theory over finite chain rings but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Note On "The Volume Of Random Simplices From Elliptical Distributions In High Dimension"
authors: Li Yanpeng Shan Xizheng
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work by Gusakova et al. (Stochastic Process. Appl. 164 (2023) 357-382) has shown a central and a stable limit theorem for the logarithmic volume of random simplices and random convex bodies under an elliptical framework in the high dimensional regime, that is, if p and n tend to infinity in such a way that the ratio tends to \gamma within (0,1). A technical condition (Equation (2.6) of Assumption (B) therein) requires that the population matrix AA* is close in Frobenius norm to a multiple of the identity matrix, which is rather restrictive and rules out various settings for statistical application, such as spiked models and dependent structure models. In this note we offer a general relaxation of this condition, which arrives at a reasonable condition and covers numerous scenarios, as well as consequences for the volume of general random simplices and random convex bodies. In particular, our results covers the Toeplitz/AR(1) covariance structures studied by Jiang and Pham (Ann. Stat. 53 (2025) 907-928), giving a concrete application of our theorem to high-dimensional dependent covariance models.
tldr: This note relaxes a technical condition in a limit theorem for random simplices from elliptical distributions, extending results to high-dimensional dependent covariance models.
motivation: The original condition required the population matrix to be close to a multiple of the identity, which is restrictive and excludes many statistical models like spiked or dependent structures.
method: The authors relax the Frobenius norm condition to a more general assumption and prove central and stable limit theorems for the logarithmic volume of random simplices under the new condition.
result: The relaxed condition covers Toeplitz/AR(1) covariance structures, providing a concrete application to high-dimensional dependent covariance models.
conclusion: The note generalizes previous results, making them applicable to a wider class of elliptical distributions and covariance structures.

title: Lib-trap: Standard Cell Library Hardware Trojan Risk Assessment And Prevention
authors: Harish Kumar Dharavath, Md Muhtasim Alam Chowdhury, Rozhin Yasaei, Soheil Salehi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerabilities inherent to the fabless semiconductor manufacturing model have significantly increased the risk of malicious Hardware Trojan (HT) insertion, posing severe threats to hardware security. Several HT mitigation and detection strategies have been developed, and existing works explore the insertion of HTs in the space between standard cells in an integrated circuit. However, there is a lack of research into the vulnerabilities posed by the building blocks of most digital designs on the market today, the standard cells. This work investigates a novel threat model in which standard cells are considered untrusted. Our proposed threat model provides the design house with a tampered standard cell library. The intended netlist is synthesized and implemented using the tampered library. During fabrication, a nefarious foundry replaces the library's deactivated HT cells with activated counterparts. Using open-source and industry-standard Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools, existing standard cell libraries, Saed32nm and Sky130nm, are converted into malicious libraries capable of masking the presence of arbitrary HTs from IC designers. The malicious library is then applied and characterized in multiple standard benchmark designs. To demonstrate the efficacy and stealthiness of this standard cell-based attack vector, three benchmark circuits, an AES-128 encryption core, an Ethernet controller, and a WISHBONE DMA engine, were synthesized using both clean and Trojan-infected libraries across Synopsys 32nm and SkyWater 130nm technologies. Design-level features, including total cell count, total area, dynamic power consumption, and static power, were extracted from these synthesized circuits to serve as inputs for binary classification.
tldr: This paper proposes a hardware Trojan threat model where standard cell libraries are tampered with, and demonstrates its feasibility using EDA tools.
motivation: The fabless semiconductor model increases risk of hardware Trojan insertion, and existing research overlooks vulnerabilities in standard cells.
method: The authors convert clean standard cell libraries into malicious ones using open-source and industry-standard EDA tools, then synthesize benchmark circuits with both clean and Trojan-infected libraries.
result: The malicious libraries can mask arbitrary hardware Trojans, and design-level features (cell count, area, power) are extracted for binary classification.
conclusion: Standard cell libraries pose a significant security risk, and the proposed threat model highlights the need for new detection and prevention methods.

title: VeriChat: An Agentic Conversational Ai Assistant For Hardware Security Verification
authors: Dipayan Saha, Khan Thamid Hasan, Shams Tarek, Sujan Kumar Saha, Mark Tehranipoor, Farimah Farahmandi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hardware security verification is a multi-stage process in which engineers must navigate complex design analyses, threat considerations, and verification strategies. They often need security-focused guidance, yet current verification environments provide little structured support for such assistance. Although conversational AI could offer such on-demand assistance, directly using general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT or Gemini is risky due to their tendency to hallucinate and their reliance on static, outdated knowledge. We present VeriChat, a domain-specialized conversational assistant designed to support, rather than replace, existing verification workflows by providing context-aware security guidance. VeriChat employs a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent workflow in which three specialized agents collaboratively minimize hallucinations while improving the transparency and reliability of the response. Beyond question answering, VeriChat integrates open-source EDA tools, including Icarus Verilog, Yosys, and SymbiYosys, to perform syntax checking, synthesis analysis, simulation, and formal verification directly on user-provided RTL designs. Evaluated using a comprehensive methodology, VeriChat achieves a Faithfulness score of 87.73%, significantly outperforming the leading proprietary models. We demonstrate the framework through a hardware Trojan detection case study on an AES S-Box IP, where VeriChat autonomously identifies, simulates, and formally proves a covert key-leakage vulnerability through a multi-turn conversational workflow.
tldr: VeriChat is a conversational AI assistant for hardware security verification, using retrieval-augmented multi-agent workflow and EDA tools to assist engineers.
motivation: Hardware security verification is complex and current environments lack structured support; general-purpose chatbots hallucinate and have outdated knowledge.
method: VeriChat employs three specialized agents with retrieval-augmented generation and integrates open-source EDA tools for syntax checking, synthesis, simulation, and formal verification.
result: Achieves 87.73% Faithfulness score, outperforming proprietary models; demonstrated via hardware Trojan detection on an AES S-Box IP.
conclusion: VeriChat provides reliable, context-aware security guidance for hardware verification workflows.

title: Has This Checkpoint Been Abliterated? A Two-Signal Audit And Its Failure Map
authors: Gabriel Hurtado
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a platform tell, before deployment, whether an open-weight checkpoint has had its refusal mechanism stripped? Runtime guards cannot: they score generations, not the artifact. We combine two cheap internal signals, a reference-anchored activation refusal-gap and a weight-recovery energy of the base-to-candidate weight difference, into a threshold-free checkpoint audit. The two are negatively correlated and label-complementary: the gap supplies refusal-specificity and the weight energy supplies recall. On a 273-checkpoint registry spanning Qwen, DeepSeek-distilled Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, their z-sum separates 57 public abliterations from 37 benign fine-tunes, merges, and instruction-tunes at AUROC 0.95, significantly above either signal alone (0.84, 0.90), and a Youden-calibrated threshold transfers to held-out families at balanced accuracy 0.89 (FPR 0.11), missing only 4 of 57. We then map two failures, in order of severity: a spoofed reference evades both axes with no training ({\Delta}W=0, =1 by construction), and a white-box owner trains a checkpoint past the threshold while it stays guard-unsafe and coherent. The audit is effective triage, not tamper-proofing: it presumes an attested reference, and its claims are bounded by the registry we evaluate it on.
tldr: This paper proposes a two-signal audit to detect whether an open-weight AI checkpoint has had its refusal mechanism removed, achieving high accuracy on a registry of 273 checkpoints.
motivation: Platforms need to verify before deployment whether a checkpoint has been 'abliterated' (refusal removed), as runtime guards only score generations and not the artifact itself.
method: The audit combines a reference-anchored activation refusal-gap and a weight-recovery energy of the base-to-candidate weight difference into a threshold-free z-sum statistic.
result: On a 273-checkpoint registry, the z-sum separates 57 abliterations from 37 benign modifications at AUROC 0.95, outperforming either signal alone (0.84, 0.90).
conclusion: The audit is effective as triage but not tamper-proof; it assumes an attested reference and has bounded claims based on the registry.

title: Sign In The Air To Unlock: An Interface For Authentication In Virtual And Augmented Reality Powered By Point-Voxel Cross-Attention Network
authors: Neda Abdolrahimi, Thiru Siddharth, Frank Sicongchen, Vir V Phoha
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01435v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Significant advancement of immersive technologies such as Virtual and Augmented Reality (VR/AR) and their integration into diverse aspects of modern life need authentication interfaces that are secure, intuitive, and compatible with embodied interaction. Traditional methods such as passwords, PINs, and device-based logins, break immersion and rely on external hardware. Recent 3D-specific behavioral approaches, such as hand-gesture, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG)-based methods, offer promising alternatives but often require specialized sensors or constrain natural movement, limiting usability in dynamic environments. We present Sign in the Air to Unlock, an in-air signature interface that enables users to authenticate by signing naturally in 3D space which is a familiar, personal, and reproducible gesture. To realize this interface, we design a point-voxel Cross-Attention Network (PV-Net) that jointly models local motion dynamics and global spatial structure from 3D trajectories. The model is evaluated on two datasets: the public DeepAirSig dataset (1,800 signatures from 40 users) and ImmAirsig, a new dataset collected using Meta Quest 2 in immersive VR (880 samples from 22 users). PV-Net achieves an Equal Error Rate of 2.5% on DeepAirSig and 76% classification accuracy on ImmAirSig. These findings highlight the potential of 3D behavioral interfaces for seamless, user-centric authentication that merges security with natural interaction in immersive environments.
tldr: This paper presents an in-air signature authentication interface for VR/AR using a point-voxel cross-attention network.
motivation: Traditional authentication methods break immersion in VR/AR, and existing 3D behavioral approaches require specialized sensors or constrain movement.
method: The authors design a point-voxel Cross-Attention Network (PV-Net) that jointly models local motion dynamics and global spatial structure from 3D trajectories.
result: PV-Net achieves an Equal Error Rate of 2.5% on DeepAirSig and 76% classification accuracy on ImmAirSig.
conclusion: 3D behavioral interfaces like in-air signatures can provide secure, intuitive authentication in immersive environments.

title: kNNGuard: Turning Llm Hidden Activations Into A Training-Free Configurable Guardrail
authors: Mahmoud Abdelfattah, Hamid Nasiri, Peter Garraghan
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02072v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in domains requiring guardrails to detect unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts. Existing guardrails predominately rely on fine-tuning to build classifiers, which often suffer from low generalization and high inference latency. We present kNNGuard, a training-free guardrail that utilizes the activation space of an off-the-shelf LLM. Given a small bank of 50 safe and unsafe prompts, kNNGuard extracts hidden activations and performs multi-layer kNN fusing activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification. Across six domains spanning topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails while running 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail, and 10x faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier without gradient updates or fine-tuning. Domain adaptation requires only updating the labeled bank, which can be constructed in under 10 seconds and several orders of magnitude faster than established guardrails. We also analyze the impact of system prompts, layer selection, and integration into production LLM pipelines as a configurable, low-latency guardrail.
tldr: This paper presents a training-free guardrail for LLMs using k-nearest neighbors on hidden activations.
motivation: Existing guardrails rely on fine-tuning, which suffers from low generalization and high latency; a training-free alternative is needed.
method: kNNGuard extracts hidden activations from an off-the-shelf LLM and performs multi-layer kNN fusing activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification.
result: It achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned guardrails while running 2.7x faster, and domain adaptation requires only updating a small labeled bank.
conclusion: kNNGuard offers a configurable, low-latency guardrail solution without gradient updates or fine-tuning.

title: Near-Term Emission Targets Need Immediate Attention In The Usa
authors: Trevor Barnes, Kamran Tehranchi, Brad Reinholz, Malcolm Metcalfe, Taco Niet
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given recent changes in federal climate policy, the United States is unlikely to meet its original 2030 Paris Agreement emission target of a 50-52% reduction from 2005 levels. However, rapid near-term abatement remains achievable through targeted multi-sector energy transitions. Extending the open-source energy system model, PyPSA-USA, to perform multi-sector analysis, we evaluate the primary drivers of USA energy costs and emissions though applying global sensitivity analysis. Our results suggest that fossil fuel price volatility is the dominant driver of marginal electricity and energy costs across most of the nation, however, uncoordinated state-level renewable mandates can induce localized cost spikes due to regional bottlenecks. We find that system climate impact (CO2e) is overwhelming sensitive to fugitive methane leakage rates and global warming potential assumptions. Addressing upstream methane leaks will play a crucial role in abating climate-related damages. Finally, demand-side electrification, specifically light-duty electric vehicles and service sector heating, can act as immediate levers for carbon abatement.
