To handle in-band semantic abuse, ElephantAgent additionally provides Historical Traceability, enabling conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.
tldr: This paper proposes a protocol for ensuring contextual state continuity in agentic systems using trusted hardware and linearizable ledgers.
motivation: Agentic systems are vulnerable to tool and memory poisoning attacks that can covertly bias agent behavior due to lack of verifiable continuity in contextual state.
method: ElephantAgent recomputes a digest of the local contextual state before each query and verifies it against an authorized digest maintained on replicated trusted hardware, with a linearizable ledger of state transitions.
result: The protocol detects out-of-band state tampering and provides historical traceability for post-hoc audit and recovery.
conclusion: ElephantAgent enforces contextual state continuity to defend against poisoning attacks in agentic systems.

title: Towards A Phonology-Informed Evaluation Of Multilingual Tts
authors: Sneha Ray Barman, Neeraj Kumar Sharma, Shakuntala Mahanta
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01965v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural TTS systems can sound natural across languages, but naturalness does not guarantee the preservation of sound contrasts that distinguish words from their grammatical forms. Standard metrics like MOS do not test for this. We propose a classifier-based framework that audits TTS output against language-specific phonological patterns using human speech as a benchmark. Testing Assamese advanced tongue root (ATR) vowel harmony with Meta's MMS TTS, we show that a classifier trained on human speech transfers to synthesized speech with minimal loss. The faithfulness audit reveals that [+ATR] mid vowels are realized as [-ATR] in 1/3 tokens despite an underlying [+ATR] specification, a bias absent in human speech. At the word level, predicted ATR labels classify harmony more accurately than transcription labels, indicating a gap between intended and produced phonology. The framework offers task-specific diagnostics and generalizes to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic cues.
tldr: This paper proposes a phonology-informed evaluation framework for multilingual TTS, focusing on Assamese vowel harmony.
motivation: Standard metrics like MOS do not test whether TTS preserves sound contrasts that distinguish grammatical forms.
method: A classifier trained on human speech is used to audit TTS output against language-specific phonological patterns.
result: The audit reveals that [+ATR] mid vowels are realized as [-ATR] in 1/3 tokens, a bias absent in human speech.
conclusion: The framework offers task-specific diagnostics and generalizes to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic cues.

title: Fine-Grained Bounds For Courcelle's Theorem
authors: Daniel Lokshtanov, Fahad Panolan, Saket Saurabh, Jie Xue, Meirav Zehavi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02033v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Courcelle's theorem states that there exists an algorithm that takes as input a graph [MATH] of treewidth at most [MATH] and a MSO formula [MATH], and determines whether [MATH] satisfies [MATH] in time [MATH]. It is folklore that the the function [MATH] contains a tower of exponentials whose height depends as a linear function of the number of quantifier alternations of the input formula [MATH]. A classic reduction of Frick and Grohe shows that, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), the linear growth of the height of the tower is unavoidable. Nevertheless, there is still a huge gap between existing upper and lower bounds -- after all, there is quite a difference between a single exponential and a double exponential running time. In addition, this only gives us a very coarse understanding in the time complexity of Courcelle's theorem. In this paper, we prove a fine-grained version of Courcelle's theorem with nearly ETH-tight dependence on the treewidth parameter [MATH] and the quantifier structure of [MATH] (specifically, the number of first order and second order variables in each quantifier alternation block).
tldr: This paper proves fine-grained complexity bounds for Courcelle's theorem on graphs of bounded treewidth, with nearly tight dependence on treewidth and quantifier structure.
motivation: Courcelle's theorem has a huge gap between known upper and lower bounds; the goal is to obtain a more precise understanding of the time complexity.
method: The authors develop a fine-grained version of Courcelle's theorem using a reduction framework and complexity-theoretic arguments, achieving nearly ETH-tight bounds.
result: They provide nearly tight lower and upper bounds on the running time as a function of treewidth and the quantifier alternation structure of the MSO formula.
conclusion: The work significantly narrows the gap in our understanding of Courcelle's theorem's complexity, but remains within computational complexity theory without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: HaloGuard 1.0: An Open Weights Constitutional Classifier For Multilingual Ai Safety
authors: Navaneeth Sangameswaran, Preetham S, Ashmiya Lenin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02079v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present HaloGuard 1.0, an open-weights implementation of the constitutional-classifier paradigm for input safety. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on English and multilingual prompt-safety benchmarks at roughly one-tenth the model size of current leading open guard models. The safety constitution is the organising structure of the corpus: a natural-language constitution of 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories drives synthetic data generation, with exhaustive one-to-one paired counterfactuals that hold topic and vocabulary fixed while flipping intent, a two-tier harmless design that separately targets boundary and baseline false positives (FPs), and balanced multilingual materialisation across 46 languages that treats language as a surface form appearing on both sides of the boundary rather than as an adversarial signal. Across seven prompt-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B attains the best average F1 (90.9) of any open guard we evaluate, outperforming baselines up to 27B parameters (over 30 times larger) while holding false-positive rate (FPR) to 4.3 and false-negative rate (FNR) to 9.5. The HaloGuard 1.0-4B variant reaches average F1 of 92.1 and FPR of 3.5, spending its extra capacity on precision rather than recall. A structured adjudication of the remaining failures indicates that most apparent missed-harm cases are benchmark mislabels rather than genuine model misses. An always-on adversarial red-teaming protocol continuously hardens the guard against both content-level and agentic attacks. We release the models as open weights.
tldr: HaloGuard 1.0 is an open-weights constitutional classifier for multilingual AI safety, achieving state-of-the-art prompt-safety benchmarks with a small model size.
motivation: The paper aims to provide an efficient and effective open-weights guard model for detecting harmful prompts in multiple languages, addressing the need for scalable AI safety solutions.
method: The authors use a natural-language constitution of 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories to drive synthetic data generation, with paired counterfactuals and a two-tier harmless design to reduce false positives, and balanced multilingual data across 46 languages.
result: HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B achieves an average F1 of 90.9 on seven benchmarks, outperforming models up to 27B parameters, with low false-positive and false-negative rates.
conclusion: The model demonstrates that small, constitution-driven classifiers can match or exceed larger models in prompt safety, and continuous red-teaming further hardens the guard against attacks.
